@Pro-Coder04 , I'm fairly new to it as well. Perhaps @phofl or @datapythonista could point you in the right direction. If I had to guess, I bet it is related to the recent version update of the API documentation theme (see #48285) and not directly in pandas code. The documentation pages are autogenerated from a package called "Sphinx", the API pages are defined in `/doc/source/reference` and it uses a configuration defined in `/doc/source/conf.py`.

Happy to get the `Show source` link removed, doesn't seem it's working for the API, and not sure in what cases this can be useful.
I think this should be done in our `conf.py` file, see the docs of the theme here: https://pydata-sphinx-theme.readthedocs.io/en/stable/user_guide/source-buttons.html

CC: @jorisvandenbossche, I guess you added this when we started using the pydata theme, probably it's just the default

Looks like pydata-sphinx-theme added a default `sourcelink.html` component around June of this year (See https://github.com/pydata/pydata-sphinx-theme/pull/714), which makes their documentation incomplete. I believe the correct way to remove it is now to set `html_show_sourcelink = False` in the `conf.py`.

Alternative option is to override the `sourcelink.html` template and have it point to our current "[source]" link.

Thanks for the request - as another alternative for pyarrow, you can use `ArrowExtensionArray`.

```python
s = pd.Series([uuid4().bytes], dtype=pd.ArrowDtype(pa.uuid()))
print(s)
# 0    b'\xee\xfb+\xd0\x0bOKd\x85d\xa1\xd6\xf4\x1eY\x1e'
# dtype: extension<arrow.uuid>[pyarrow]
```

It's not clear to me what benefit a custom EA has over this.
See “Alternative Solutions” point 2.

Perhaps I'm misunderstanding - you're proposing to add an EA specifically for PyArrow-backed UUID data, is that right? It's not clear what advantage that would have over the current `ArrowExtensionArray`.

The NumPy case is clear.

Ah got it! You’re basically suggesting “Alternative Solution 2b”: Only add the numpy EA but keep the unspecific pyarrow one.

Wrapping the pyarrow case has smaller benefits. Most importantly, the behavior of the two storage backends could be more transparent, and people could just create a `dtype="uuid"` and not care about behavioral differences, just like they can now with `dtype="string"` arrays.

Some specific advantages:
- (un)boxing has many convenience benefits, like allowing `if my_uuid in pyarrow_backed:` and so on instead of manually converting objects to `pyarrow.UuidScalar` (e.g. in your code `s[0] in s` evaluates to `False`)
- element-wise comparisons between the numpy version and pyarrow version would work (maybe partially possible by implementing everything on the numpy EA side?)
- currently doing `pd.Series(pa.array(..., type=pa.uuid()))` creates a series with object dtype instead of the extension dtype
- We should display UUIDs using the canonical UUID representation, as opposed to the output of your example

Some advantages might be obtainable by special-casing some code paths in `ArrowExtensionArray`, like we do for timestamps, but it’s unclear to me why we chose to do that for timestamps while having a subclass for strings, and where to draw the line.

What’s there in pandas is less usable than I thought, I couldn’t figure out at all how to make `__contains__` work without accessing `_pa_array` directly:

So `s[0]` conveniently unboxes to a `uuid.UUID` object, but then?

```pycon
>>> s[0] in s
False  # Should be True!
>>> pa.scalar(s[0].bytes, type=pa.uuid()) in s
False  # Should be True?
>>> s[0] in s.array
NotImplementedError: extension<arrow.uuid>
>>> pa.scalar(s[0].bytes, type=pa.uuid()) in s.array
NotImplementedError: eq not implemented for <class 'pyarrow.lib.UuidScalar'>
>>> pa.scalar(s[0].bytes, type=pa.uuid()) in s.array._pa_array
True  # but at what cost?
```

All this might be fixable generically (maybe fixing the `NotImplementedError`s makes the rest work), but point is, none of does yet, and with some APIs simply returning the wrong result instead of erroring, it’s not super reassuring to use.

Thanks for the report! Confirmed on main. Due to groupby always returning `NaN` (see https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/48476 for more on this), the group in question has the value `NaN`. With this, the issue is here:

https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/d8159471b1e6e9327274a1b98aca2b88c9b5e0b5/pandas/core/groupby/groupby.py#L691

We are using `dict.get` with `name` being `NaN`, but you cannot reliable access `NaN` as a key in a dictionary since `NaN == NaN` gives False.

Further investigations and PRs to fix are welcome!

Hi, I had a shot at it. In order to make it work we can replace the keys that are `NaN` with `np.nan` in `self.inidices`. So essentially I think this is a simplified example of what you could do before:

```python
>>> df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, np.nan, 3], "b": [np.nan, 20, 30]})
>>> df["a"].update(df["b"])
>>> df
      a     b
0   1.0   NaN
1  20.0  20.0
2  30.0  30.0

```

With pandas 2.3, that gives a FutureWarning, with pandas 3.0 that gives a ChainedAssignmentError (warning, here can definitely still update the warning message)

So, what is the best alternative to achieve the same?

Richard mentioned the following, but this requires an intermediate variable (which I find a bit unfortunate):

```python
>>> df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, np.nan, 3], "b": [np.nan, 20, 30]})
>>> ser = df["a"]
>>> ser.update(df["b"])
>>> df["a"] = ser
>>> df
      a     b
0   1.0   NaN
1  20.0  20.0
2  30.0  30.0
```

To avoid that, you can call this method on the dataframe directly, however because that aligns the input df, you have to rename it first:

```python
>>> df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, np.nan, 3], "b": [np.nan, 20, 30]})
>>> df.update(df[["b"]].rename(columns={"b": "a"}))
>>> df
      a     b
0   1.0   NaN
1  20.0  20.0
2  30.0  30.0
```

or a bit simpler (I only thought about this wondering if this wouldn't make it simpler if we supported that. Turns out we do, because that is coerced to a dataframe):

```python
>>> df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, np.nan, 3], "b": [np.nan, 20, 30]})
>>> df.update({"a": df["b"]})
>>> df
      a     b
```

I've put together a very scrappy first attempt. I used .sample() as the base but have adapted it to sample a single index randomly and then return the next n items including that idx.

It supports random state, but not much else yet. I would like some feedback on the approach and the overall feature from the maintainers before continuing with this feature.  I haven't included edge case handling yet, but the idea I think is as .sample() - raise a ValueError is n exceeds length of object.

```Python
def sample_window(
            self,
            n: int | None = None,
            axis: Axis | None = None,
            random_state: RandomState | None = None,
    ) -> Self:
        """
        Return a contiguous window of items from the object. The startint point of the window is randomly selected.

        Selects a random index and will return the next `n` items in the axis.

        You can use `random_state` for reproducibility.

        Parameters
        ----------
        n : int, optional
            Number of items from axis to return in the window.
            Default = 1
        random_state : int, array-like, BitGenerator, np.random.RandomState, np.random.Generator, optional
            If int, array-like, or BitGenerator, seed for random number generator.
            If np.random.RandomState or np.random.Generator, use as given.
            Default ``None`` results in sampling with the current state of np.random.
        axis : {0 or 'index', 1 or 'columns', None}, default None
            Axis to sample. Accepts axis number or name. Default is stat axis
            for given data type. For `Series` this parameter is unused and defaults to `None`.

        Returns
        -------
        Series or DataFrame
            A new object of same type as caller containing a contiguous window `n` items
            randomly from the caller object.

        Notes
        -----

        To ensure the window can be sampled we sample the random index from the range [0, len(axis) - n].

        Examples
        --------
        >>> df = pd.DataFrame(
        ...     {
        ...         "num_legs": [2, 4, 8, 0],
        ...         "num_wings": [2, 0, 0, 0],
        ...         "num_specimen_seen": [10, 2, 1, 8],
        ...     },
        ...     index=["falcon", "dog", "spider", "fish"],
        ... )
        >>> df
                num_legs  num_wings  num_specimen_seen
        falcon         2          2                 10
        dog            4          0                  2
        spider         8          0                  1
        fish           0          0                  8

        Sample a contiguous window of size 2. Note that we use `random_state`
        to ensure the reproducibility of the examples.

        >>> df.sample_window(2, random_state=1)
                num_legs  num_wings  num_specimen_seen
        dog            4          0                  2
        spider         8          0                  1

        """
        if axis is None:
            axis = 0

        axis = self._get_axis_number(axis)
        obj_len = self.shape[axis]

        # Process random_state argument
        rs = common.random_state(random_state)

        valid_range = obj_len - n

        print(f"obj_len: {obj_len} n: {n} valid_range: {valid_range}")

        # User defines what size window they want then function will take random sample from which the next N is valid for that size
        # e.g. if n = 10, len(df) == 100, then sample from 0-90
        sampled_index = rs.randint(0, valid_range + 1)  # sample.sample(valid_range, 1, False, None, rs).item()

        # Sampled indices has to be a list of valid indices
        sampled_indices = [sampled_index + i for i in range(n)]

        print(f"Sampled index: {sampled_index} - sampled_indices: {sampled_indices}")

        result = self.take(sampled_indices, axis=axis)

        return result
```

This seems to be specifically an issue in `align` when the other operand is a DataFrame instead of a series

```python
>>> ser1 = pd.Series(index=["a", "b"])
>>> ser2 = pd.Series(index=range(3))
>>> res1, res2 = ser1.align(ser2, join="left")
>>> res1.index
Index(['a', 'b'], dtype='str')
>>> res1, res2 = ser1.align(pd.DataFrame({0: ser2}), join="left")
>>> res1.index
Index(['a', 'b'], dtype='object')
```

And the align behaviour boils down to:

```python
>>> idx_str = pd.Index(["a", "b"], dtype=str)
>>> idx_obj = pd.Index(["a", "b"], dtype=object)
>>> 
>>> idx_str.join(idx_obj, how="left")
Index(['a', 'b'], dtype='object')
```

So the question here is whether this is actually the expected behaviour. In doing `res = s.str.cat(pd.Series(["A", "B", "C"]), sep=",", na_rep="-")`, you are passing a Series with an integer range index to `cat()`. At that point we have an operation between an object with str index vs integer range index. The common dtype for those is `object` dtype. In that sense, this is the expected behaviour.

However, since this is doing a "left" index join, one could expect that it is doing a bit more work to preserve the left index' dtype if there is no overlap. At the moment we don't special case such a left join without overlap, though. For example also an integer index gets cast to object:

```python
>>> pd.Index([1, 2, 3])
Index([1, 2, 3], dtype='int64')
>>> pd.Index([1, 2, 3]).join(pd.Index(["a", "b"]))
Index([1, 2, 3], dtype='object')
```
Closely related: https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/62949

I've opened PR #63485 to fix this issue.

The root cause was `Index.join()` losing StringDtype on left joins when there's no overlap with the other index. The fix preserves StringDtype when:
- Join method is "left"
- Left index has StringDtype  
- Right index does NOT have StringDtype
- No overlap exists (join result equals left index)

This minimal change ensures `str.cat(Series)` now preserves the StringDtype index as expected, while maintaining backward compatibility for cases with actual overlap.

The question becomes how much is too much, especially considering how many users run into problems. It seems to me, just based on my own experience, that for 99.9% of usages, pandas current algorithm is sufficient. That said, if there are improvements that could improve stability without significant performance or maintenance cost, I think they can definitely be considered.

That's a pretty valid concern. My take is that we should fully support float64 in all use cases. Currently, there are certain places where multiplying two large float64s would cause over/underflow and output the wrong values (Pearson Correlation using Welford). We should do what we can to minimize these instances if possible. I wouldn't expect us to need to implement anything past double-double to cover all such scenarios. 

The alternative concern is that different functions running into the current issues would have varying implementations to offset the precision limitation, this would make the code harder to maintain overall. For example, I know that re-centering the Pearson calculations can limit the precision loss, but would prefer not to if possible as it would add an unnecessary layer of complexity vs just adding specialized operators where needed.

this is a small prototype to show the behavior i had in mind. missing values are filled using nearby observations in time, limited by a user-defined window. within that window, closer points get more weight, and past vs future doesn’t matter, only temporal distance. this feels more natural for irregularly spaced data than ffill/bfill, and avoids interpolation semantics.

i also looked at PeriodIndex logic in pandas/core/indexes/period.py to get a feel for how pandas handles windows and time-based operations. (sketched with a little help from an ai model.)

```
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

def nearest_in_time_fill(
    s: pd.Series,
    kind: str = "num",
    window: int | None = None,
    weighting: float = 1.0,
) -> pd.Series:
    if not isinstance(s.index, pd.DatetimeIndex):
        raise TypeError("DatetimeIndex required")
    out = s.copy()
    t = s.index.asi8

    missing = s.isna().values
    t_known = t[~missing]
    v_known = `s.values[~missing]`

    for i in np.where(missing)[0]:
        d = np.abs(t_known - t[i])

        if window is not None:
            use = d <= window
            if not use.any():
                continue
            d, v = d[use], v_known[use]
        else:
            v = v_known

        if kind == "num":
            w = 1 / np.maximum(d, 1) ** weighting
            out.iloc[i] = np.average(v.astype(float), weights=w)
        else:
            out.iloc[i] = v[d == d.min()][0]

    return out

```

Thanks for the report. I'm seeing a couple of options:

1. Use `pandas.core.dtypes.cast.find_common_type` to convert both caller and `value` to a compatible dtype.
2. Raise on any dtype mismatch; make the user handle.
3. Raise in certain cases based on the result of `pandas.core.dtypes.cast.find_common_type` (e.g. object).

@kerrf - if you see other possible solutions, feel free to surface them. Further investigations are welcome!
I'm working on this issue

I think the approach should be 
dispatching directly to the underlying `_data` (int64) array—is **superior to the `find_common_type` suggestion** for this specific case.

By unwrapping the `IntegerArray` to its raw numpy backing, we avoid the "common type" trap entirely:
1.  We stay in `int64` land, avoiding the silent precision loss of `float64` (which caused the bug at $2^{53}$).
2.  We avoid the massive overhead of casting to `object` dtype, which would be the only other "safe" common type.
3.  We solve the issue without raising `TypeError` on valid data.

This treats `IntegerArray` as a first-class citizen with its own optimized path, rather than coercing it.

@sanrishi - the int64 array will hold values that you do not want to impact the result.

```python
ser = pd.Series([1, 2, 3], dtype="Int64")
ser.iloc[1] = pd.NA
print(ser)
# 0       1
# 1    <NA>
# 2       3
# dtype: Int64
print(ser.array._data)
# [1 2 3]
```

You do not want `2` impacting the result in this case. How do you handle this?

In addition, the proposed logic indeed seems too specific for this particular case.

That is a great point regarding the "ghost" values in the underlying array. You are absolutely right that accessing `_data` blindly is unsafe because of those stale values.

The way to handle this—and keep the precision benefit—is to **apply the mask before searching**.

Instead of passing the raw `_data` directly to `searchsorted`, we slice it using the boolean mask first:
`valid_values = arr._data[~arr._mask]`

For your example `[1, <NA>, 3]`, this effectively passes `[1, 3]` to the search function. This completely ignores the hidden `2` (garbage value) and ensures `searchsorted` only sees the valid, sorted integers.

This way, we avoid the garbage data *and* the float precision loss.

Just passing a read-only array to numpy's `permutation()` works fine in general:

```python
>>> arr = np.array(['foo', 'bar', 'baz'], dtype=object)
>>> arr.flags.writeable = False
>>> rng = np.random.default_rng()
>>> rng.permutation(arr)
array(['baz', 'foo', 'bar'], dtype=object)
```

and for the case of `copy=None`, both the numpy-backed and pyarrow-backed string array gives a read-only result in `__array__`:

```python
>>> s = pd.Series(["foo", "bar", "baz"], dtype=pd.StringDtype())
>>> np.asarray(s).flags.writeable
False
>>> s = pd.Series(["foo", "bar", "baz"], dtype=pd.StringDtype("python"))
>>> np.asarray(s).flags.writeable
False
```

> So I'm not exactly sure
> 
> 1. If NumPy in their docs defines "copy" as an explicit deep copy or if the `None` convention is appropriate
> 2. If pandas should interpreting `copy=None` in a different manner for this case

The numpy docs on this topic ([here](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/user/basics.interoperability.html#the-array-method)) seem clear: `copy=None` should only copy if the `dtype` requires it, and otherwise be treated as "no copy if not needed". So in that sense, I think the pandas behaviour is currently correct.

I suppose it has more to do with our logic of marking the resulting array as read-only because of CoW (https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/63099), and the slight differences between the numpy vs pyarrow backed string array (eg in case of pyarrow, the chunked array `to_numpy()` first creates a 2d array of which it takes a 1d view to return, and seems to matter).

Trying some simplified reproducers to try to understand why this is happening, it seems quite subtle changes can trigger / not trigger the issue:

```python
# mimicking what happens with numpy-backed StringArray -> does not trigger it
class MyArray1:
    def __init__(self):
        self.arr = np.array(['foo', 'bar', 'baz'], dtype=object)

    def __array__(self, dtype=None, copy=None):
        arr = self.arr.view()
        arr.flags.writeable = False
        print(arr.flags, arr.base.flags)
        return arr

>>> arr = MyArray1()
>>> rng.permutation(arr)
array(['baz', 'bar', 'foo'], dtype=object)

# mimicking what happens with pyarrow-backed StringArray -> triggers it
class MyArray2:
    def __init__(self):
        self.arr = pa.chunked_array([['foo', 'bar', 'baz']])

    def __array__(self, dtype=None, copy=None):
        arr = self.arr.to_numpy()
        arr = arr.view()
        arr.flags.writeable = False
        return arr

>>> arr = MyArray2()
>>> rng.permutation(arr)
...
ValueError: array is read-only

# mimicking the same but without pyarrow -> still triggers it
class MyArray3:
    def __array__(self, dtype=None, copy=None):
        arr2d = np.array([['foo', 'bar', 'baz']], dtype=object)
        arr = arr2d[0].view()
        arr.flags.writeable = False
        return arr

>>> arr = MyArray3()
>>> rng.permutation(arr)
...
ValueError: array is read-only

# Simplifying further -> now essentially back to first example, except we are not keeping the initial array alive on the object 
# -> for some reason still triggers it
class MyArray4:
    def __array__(self, dtype=None, copy=None):
        arr = np.array(['foo', 'bar', 'baz'], dtype=object)
        arr = arr.view()
        arr.flags.writeable = False
        print(arr.flags, arr.base, arr.base.flags)
        return arr

>>> arr = MyArray4()
>>> rng.permutation(arr)
...

```

So it seems to be related to the array having a `.base` that is an actual live object or not?


Another thing to note is that there is something inside `permutation` that works differently for objects with `__array__`, because if we call `asarray` first explicitly, then it does not happen:

```python
>>> s = pd.Series(["foo", "bar", "baz"], dtype=pd.StringDtype())
>>> rng.permutation(s)
...
ValueError: array is read-only
>>> rng.permutation(np.asarray(s))
array(['foo', 'bar', 'baz'], dtype=object)
```

It seems that numpy's `permutation` tries to do a copy with `np.array(arr)` here: https://github.com/numpy/numpy/blob/4900421c6d54b3db3cca89a9ace6ff563659edb3/numpy/random/_generator.pyx#L4970-L4980. But in that case it should be passing `copy=True` to `__array__`, which doesn't happen, so I suppose for some reason, in certain cases it doesn't get there (because of the `if np.may_share_memory(arr, x):`)

```python
>>> arr = MyArray1()
>>> np.may_share_memory(np.asarray(arr), arr)
True
>>> arr = MyArray4()
>>> np.may_share_memory(np.asarray(arr), arr)
False
```

And now I get the reason for this difference: when you pass an object that is not an array, it will again call `asarray()` on it. So the difference with those dummy MyArray cases and the difference between numpy vs pyarrow StringArray, is whether repeated calls of `np.asarray(arr)` return the same object. For pyarrow-backed, it gets converted to a new numpy array each time, so calling asarray twice and checking if the result shares memory does not work. 
And for the dummy MyArray cases, it thus indeed depends on whether we are creating the numpy array once and saving on the object, or creating on the fly in `__array__`.

That explains the issue finally, but also doesn't give a clear solution ... (because it is inherent to pyarrow-backed Series that the conversion to numpy can be costly, unless we would somehow cache this, at the cost of memory usage)

(except for not making the result readonly, cfr https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/63099, although this seems a case where we actually _do_ want to make the result readonly to prevent numpy to shuffle inplace)

> That explains the issue finally, but also doesn't give a clear solution ... (because it is inherent to pyarrow-backed Series that the conversion to numpy can be costly, unless we would somehow cache this, at the cost of memory usage)

Actually, not a solution to `np.may_share_memory` not working, but for the original issue about `permutation()`, we probably just need to ensure we don't mark the resulting numpy array as read-only in the case of converting a pyarrow array to numpy object array. Because in that case this is not needed, since that numpy data is already a copy, there is no need to protect it from mutation.

> I would be +1 to add a CI job with pytest-run-parallel + TSAN.

Great! One note: we're not planning to add pytest-run-parallel testing. It's often quite a bit of work to update an existing test suite to run under pytest-run-parallel. We had a Quansight intern do it for NumPy over the summer and it took them the whole internship to get a CI job set up: https://labs.quansight.org/blog/numpy-thread-safe-test-suite.

In practice many of the issues discovered this way are not reflective of real-world use of a library, mostly becaues of [this issue](https://github.com/Quansight-Labs/pytest-run-parallel/issues/14) in pytest-run-parallel. Unfortunately fixing that issue requires deep structural changes in pytest itself that @liam-devoe is thinking about. 

pytest-run-parallel *can* find real issues, but it can lead to a significant amount of churn in a test suite. The main benefit is that it gets good coverage, but it may not find the most important real-world issues.

IMO it's more intellectually challenging but less effort overall to write tests that use `threading.Thread` or `ThreadPoolExecutor` directly. IMO it's also a good idea to have tests that model parallel multithreaded workflows that library authors expect users to try and that you want to support.

Additionally, at least with NumPy, TSan + pytest-run-parallel runs is an overnight job on a beefy desktop. Pytest-xdist doesn't help much, both because each xdist worker is running its own thread pool, and because pytest-xdist itself starts to add overhead under TSan. The rule of thumb I have in my head is that a TSan-instrumented interpreter is at least 10x slower than without TSan instrumentation.

That's why for NumPy we only run a limited subset of the tests under TSan in CI and don't try to run the pytest-run-parallel tests in CI. Just one-offs every once in a while. Take a look at our CI configuration for how this is set up:

https://github.com/numpy/numpy/blob/508943d1070d8f4e0712b98db2379d49304e4e38/.github/workflows/compiler_sanitizers.yml#L109-L110

tl;dr: a pytest-run-parallel testing update is eventually probably a good idea, but I'm not proposing doing that here as a first pass.

@lionel42 in addition to what the others already explained, I think you are specifically running into https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/user_guide/migration-3-strings.html#astype-str-preserving-missing-values.

With pandas 2.3, you actually had a series with all strings, without missing values:

```python
>>> serie = pd.Series(['100A', None, '300C'])
>>> serie = serie.astype(str)
>>> serie.to_numpy()
array(['100A', 'None', '300C'], dtype=object)
>>> serie.isna()
0    False
1    False
2    False
dtype: bool
```

So the `astype(str)` converted your missing value `None` to the string `"None"`. 

Now, with pandas 3.0, `astype(str)` has been fixed to preserve missing values:

```
>>> serie = pd.Series(['100A', None, '300C'])
>>> serie = serie.astype(str)
>>> serie.isna()
0    False
1     True
2    False
dtype: bool
```

Once you have missing values, it is impossible to have all the same types when iterating over the individual values of the series, since we do not have a "missing value" of the type `str`, of the type `int`, etc

The broadcasting behavior is documented, albeit (IMO) very poorly: http://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/stable/basics.html?highlight=broadcast#matching-broadcasting-behavior

Here's a simpler demo:

```python
df = pd.DataFrame({'x': np.arange(3), 'x': np.arange(3) + 1}, index=['a', 'b', 'c'])

# explicit behavior
df.add(pd.Series([1, 10]))
df.add(pd.Series([1, 10], index=df.columns))
df.add(pd.Series([1, 10, 100], index=df.index), axis='index')

# implicit conversion behavior
df.add([1, 10])
df.add([1, 10], 'columns')
df.add([1, 10, 100], axis='index')

# DataFrame.__add__() is equivalent to DataFrame.add(..., axis='index')
df + pd.Series([1, 10], index=df.columns)
df + [1, 10]
```

As for turning the results into an array, that's just a consequence of the fact that the Series elements are arrays. The elements of the Series are broadcast according to the above, rules, and from there addition is applied naively. In this case, a number plus an array is an array, so the resulting elements are arrays.

Thanks! I do understand why it happens after digging through the code, but I would say that in an ecosystem where broadcasting is such a commonly-used pattern, it's quite confusing for a 2D object to be implicitly treated as a 1D object array containing 1D entries.

@jakevdp That's not exactly what's happening. The list on the RHS is blindly cast to `Series`, and a `Series` of `array`s is fundamentally a 1D object. It is being broadcast to form a 2D object by copying the first dimension along the second:

```
a00 a01       b0 b1
a10 a11   +   b0 b1
a20 a21       b0 b1
```

This behavior is [consistent with the behavior in NumPy](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/numpy/user/basics.broadcasting.html), where it generalizes to arbitrary dimensions.

It just so happens that, in this case, `aij` is itself an array. Pandas itself is agnostic with regard to how each `aij + bj` calculation takes place. It just so happens that there is another broadcasting step that happens between `aij` and `bj`.

I disagree that this is consistent with numpy broadcasting. Numpy implicitly treats a list of arrays as a 2D array:

```python
>>> arr = np.random.randint(0, 10, size=(3, 4))
>>> L = [np.random.randint(0, 10, 4) for i in range(3)]
>>> arr + L
array([[ 9,  6,  6, 10],
       [ 7, 13,  5,  5],
       [ 7, 15, 17,  3]])
```

2D object + 2D object = 2D object

Pandas, on the other hand, treats a list of arrays as a 1D series of anonymous objects:

```python
>>> df = pd.DataFrame(arr.T)
>>> df + L
               0              1                 2
0  [9, 8, 8, 11]  [7, 15, 6, 9]      [7, 7, 9, 3]
1   [7, 6, 6, 9]  [5, 13, 4, 7]  [15, 15, 17, 11]
2   [7, 6, 6, 9]  [6, 14, 5, 8]  [15, 15, 17, 11]
3  [8, 7, 7, 10]  [3, 11, 2, 5]      [7, 7, 9, 3]
```

Effectively, the result is 2D object + 2D object = 3D object. I found that to be quite surprising, due to the inconsistency with NumPy's behavior.

The result is even more silly if you try to add a list of series to a dataframe:

```python
>>> L = [pd.Series(row) for row in L]
>>> df + L
```

The result is a 2D dataframe, each element of which is a 1D Series, and I can't imagine a scenario in which that is what the user would want.

Since adding a list of numbers to a dataframe is basically equivalent to doing ``df[i] + L[i]`` within each column, I had expected that adding a list of Series objects to a dataframe would also be the equivalent of doing ``df[i] + L[i]`` for each column, in analogy to the way that NumPy broadcasting works (modulo the standard column-first vs. row-first difference).

Does that make sense why a user might be surprised by this behavior?

Overall, I think the biggest issue here is that this operation is doing so much implicitly, leading the user to make assumptions about what should happen... I think the most consistent option would be to make dataframe + list raise a ValueError in all cases, but that ship has probably sailed.

Lib.itemfromzerodim

Edit [rhshadrach]: lib.item_from_zerodim

I think there are two ways to handle it:

1. Consider only objects that are scalars.
2. Consider objects that can be interpreted as scalars.

Regarding the latter, any element of a 1-dimensional vector space can be considered a scalar, since in this case the vector space and its base field are isomorphic. Towards this end, `numpy`, and many other libraries, offer the [`.item()`](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.ndarray.item.html) function, which returns a scalar if the array contains exactly one element (although it doesn't seem part of the python Array API currently).

`pandas._libs.lib.is_scalar` seems to be in line here with [`numpy.isscalar`](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.isscalar.html), which also returns false for `np.array(0)`, as technically, this is considered a 0-dimensional array and hence not a scalar.

If (1) is preferred by the maintainers, this issue can probably be closed. However, `numpy.clip` does support passing 0-dimensional arrays, and so does `Series.where`, which can be used to implement `Series.clip`:

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series([-1,2,3])
s_clipped = s.where(s>np.array(0), np.array(0))
pd.testing.assert_series_equal(s_clipped, s.clip(lower=0))  # ✅
```

Whether one wants to go with option ① or ② is probably just a matter of taste/design, but using this choice consistently throughout the API seems desirable.

> but using this choice consistently throughout the API seems desirable.

Right - I'm not sure how well this is supported throughout pandas. You mentioned `clip`, but there are a number of other methods that take scalars like this I think. It seem to me the next steps are to determine which methods support this, and from that we can find a reasonable way to achieve consistency.

It's very simple. Sphinx has directives  (block level syntax) that create link targets, and roles (inline syntax) that links to these targets.

E.g. you define a module and some members:

```restructuredtext
.. module:: a.b

.. class:: Cee
.. type:: Dee
```

Afterwards you can link to all three bits:

```restructuredtext
Link to module :mod:`a.b`,
and its members :class:`a.b.Cee` and :type:`a.b.Dee`.
```

Apart from being able to link to these things in your own docs, after publishing them, others will be able to link from their docs to your link targets using  `sphinc.ext.intersphinx`. The intersphinx directory (objects.inv file) is what allows that.

I don't think so. This code ends up going through apply, which doesn't use the group selection. E.g.

```
m = pd.DataFrame(columns=["a", "b"])
gb = m.groupby(["a", "b"])
with gb._group_selection_context():
    result = gb.agg(len)
print(result.index)

MultiIndex([], names=['a', 'b'])
Index([], dtype='object')
```

This is all due to `apply` using the groupers in computation whereas `agg` doesn't.

```
m = pd.DataFrame([[1, 2], [1, 3]], columns=["a", "b"])

print(gb.apply(lambda x: x.sum()))
print(gb.agg(lambda x: x.sum()))

a      
1  2  5

a   
1  5
```

```python
def comparison_op(left: ArrayLike, right: Any, op) -> ArrayLike:
    """
    Evaluate a comparison operation `=`, `!=`, `>=`, `>`, `<=`, or `<`.

    Note: the caller is responsible for ensuring that numpy warnings are
    suppressed (with np.errstate(all="ignore")) if needed.

    Parameters
    ----------
    left : np.ndarray or ExtensionArray
    right : object
        Cannot be a DataFrame, Series, or Index.
    op : {operator.eq, operator.ne, operator.gt, operator.ge, operator.lt, operator.le}

    Returns
    -------
    ndarray or ExtensionArray
    """
    # NB: We assume extract_array has already been called on left and right
    lvalues = ensure_wrapped_if_datetimelike(left)
    rvalues = ensure_wrapped_if_datetimelike(right)

    rvalues = lib.item_from_zerodim(rvalues)

    # Special handling needed if rvalues is a zerodim np.ndarray subclass, see GH#63205
    rvalues_is_zerodim: bool = getattr(rvalues, "ndim", None) == 0

    if isinstance(rvalues, list):
        # We don't catch tuple here bc we may be comparing e.g. MultiIndex
        #  to a tuple that represents a single entry, see test_compare_tuple_strs
        rvalues = sanitize_array(rvalues, None)
    rvalues = ensure_wrapped_if_datetimelike(rvalues)

    if isinstance(rvalues, (np.ndarray, ABCExtensionArray)) and not rvalues_is_zerodim:
        # TODO: make this treatment consistent across ops and classes.
        #  We are not catching all listlikes here (e.g. frozenset, tuple)
        #  The ambiguous case is object-dtype.  See GH#27803
        if len(lvalues) != len(rvalues):
            raise ValueError(
                "Lengths must match to compare", lvalues.shape, rvalues.shape
            )

    if should_extension_dispatch(lvalues, rvalues) or (
        (isinstance(rvalues, (Timedelta, BaseOffset, Timestamp)) or right is NaT)
        and lvalues.dtype != object
    ):
        # Call the method on lvalues
        res_values = op(lvalues, rvalues)

    elif (is_scalar(rvalues) or rvalues_is_zerodim) and isna(rvalues):  # TODO: but not pd.NA?
        # numpy does not like comparisons vs None
        if op is operator.ne:
            res_values = np.ones(lvalues.shape, dtype=bool)
        else:
            res_values = np.zeros(lvalues.shape, dtype=bool)

    elif is_numeric_v_string_like(lvalues, rvalues):
        # GH#36377 going through the numexpr path would incorrectly raise
        return invalid_comparison(lvalues, rvalues, op)

    elif lvalues.dtype == object or isinstance(rvalues, str):
        res_values = comp_method_OBJECT_ARRAY(op, lvalues, rvalues)

    else:
        res_values = _na_arithmetic_op(lvalues, rvalues, op, is_cmp=True)

    return res_values
```

```
Styler.presets = [
    "red_black_cents": [('applymap', (lambda x: 'color: red' if x < 0 else 'color: black',)), ('format', ("${:.2f}",))]
]

df.style.preset("red_black_cents", subset=...)
```

essentially substitutes the `.preset` call with looking up the outlined chained items:

```
getattr(
    getattr(df.style, 
       "applymap"
    )(*(lambda x: 'color: red' if x < 0 else 'color: black',), subset=...), 
        "format"
    )(*("${:.2f}",), subset=...)
)
```

I am very opposed to creating a whole host of callable function that require individual documentation pages, e.g.

```python
df.style.preset_financial()
df.style.preset_up_arrows()
df.style.preset_accounts()
etc.
```

The concept of having one method that can branch to the named preset allows consistent treatment.

Additionally doing something like the below will break all the chaining rules because you have introduced an attribute object.
By adopting the format as suggested as above the entire method chaining is preserved - it is essentially just syntactic sugar for the existing mechanics.

```
df.style.preset.financial()
```

The idea for this functionality is inspired by kernel smoothing methods and Exponentially Weighted Moving Averages (references below):
https://corporatefinanceinstitute.com/resources/career-map/sell-side/capital-markets/exponentially-weighted-moving-average-ewma/
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kernel_smoother

Assume we have data consisting of timestamps and values:

Timestamp             ->           Value
2024-01-01 00:00  ->           10
2024-01-01 01:00  ->           12
2024-01-01 02:00  ->           13
2024-01-01 03:00  ->           16
2024-01-01 04:00  ->           19
2024-01-01 05:00  ->           20
2024-01-01 05:00  ->           26
2024-01-01 06:00  ->           22
2024-01-01 07:00  ->           24
2024-01-01 08:00 - >           27

Notes:
- Time instances are assumed to be sortable (for example using pd.to_datetime).
- Time instances may not be evenly spaced.
- Multiple values may be associated with the same timestamp (assumed to be simultaneous events).

Basic philosophy: recent values should matter more than older ones.

Step 1: Picking a window  
The user chooses a window W (for example 7 hours).

To calculate the mean at time T (say 2024-01-01 08:00), only data with:
- timestamp greater than or equal to T minus W
- timestamp strictly less than T

is considered.

This removes the first row from further processing.

Step 2: How old each data point is  
For each remaining observation, define its age as:

age = T minus timestamp

This gives:

Timestamp            -> Value  ->    Age
2024-01-01 01:00  ->   12    ->  7 hours
2024-01-01 02:00  ->   13    ->  6 hours
2024-01-01 03:00  ->   16    ->  5 hours
2024-01-01 04:00  ->   19    ->  4 hours
2024-01-01 05:00  ->   20    ->  3 hours
2024-01-01 05:00  ->   26    ->  3 hours
2024-01-01 06:00  ->   22    ->  2 hours
2024-01-01 07:00  ->   24    ->  1 hour
2024-01-01 08:00  ->   27    ->  0 hours

Step 3: Dealing with duplicate timestamps  
Observations sharing the same timestamp are assumed to be simultaneous events.

They are aggregated deterministically (for example by taking the mean), so that each timestamp contributes only once.

After this step, the data becomes:

Timestamp             ->  Value  ->  Age
2024-01-01 01:00  ->     12    ->  7 hours
2024-01-01 02:00  ->     13    ->  6 hours
2024-01-01 03:00  ->     16    ->  5 hours
2024-01-01 04:00  ->     19    ->  4 hours
2024-01-01 05:00  ->     23    ->  3 hours
2024-01-01 06:00  ->     22    ->  2 hours
2024-01-01 07:00  ->     24    ->  1 hour
2024-01-01 08:00  ->    27     ->  0 hours

Step 4: Converting age into weights  
Each observation is assigned a weight using exponential decay:

weight = exp( minus alpha times age )

Here, alpha is the decay rate:
- alpha greater than 0
- larger alpha means faster forgetting
- smaller alpha means longer retention

(The time unit for age, such as hours or days, would need to be defined.)

For this example, the weights are proportional to:
exp(-7a), exp(-6a), exp(-5a), exp(-4a), exp(-3a), exp(-2a), exp(-a), 1

Step 5: Weighted mean  
The final estimate at time T is calculated as:

weighted mean = sum(weight times value) divided by sum(weight)

For alpha approximately equal to 0.1 (which corresponds to a half-life of roughly 7 hours), the weighted mean is approximately 20.6.

For comparison, the simple mean over the same window is 19.5.

This seems reasonable, since the estimate gives more importance to recent observations rather than weighting older data equally.

```python
import functools as ft

def decay_weighted_agg(values, alpha):
    timestamps = values.index.to_series()
    weights = np.exp(-alpha * (timestamps.max() - timestamps).dt.total_seconds() / 3600)
    return (weights * values).sum() / weights.sum()

ser = pd.DataFrame(

).set_index("timestamp")["value"]
```

For (a), if we were to this to pandas I think we do not want only that as specified exactly as in https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/63551#issuecomment-3707233782. As far as `DataFrame.to_sql()` and `pd.read_sql()` are concerned, the following patch seems to provide a workaround, enabling sqlalchemy 1.4 support. I have not tested this extensively yet, it works with pandas 2.3.3,  sqlalchemy 1.4 + sqlalchemy 2.1, using a valid sqlalchemy engine connection string (tested with `sqlite://...` and `postgresql://...`)

```
try:
    # enable pandas >= 2.2 compatibility with sqlalchemy 1.4
    # -- workaround to due to https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/57049
    # -- this forces the use of pd.SQLDatabase instead of pd.SQLiteDatabase
    import pandas as pd
    import sqlalchemy as sqa

    if (Version(pd.__version__) >= Version("2.2") and
            Version(sqa.__version__) < Version("2.2")):
        from pandas.compat._optional import VERSIONS

        VERSIONS['sqlalchemy'] = '1.4'
        warnings.warn(
            "Patching pandas > 2.2 to support sqlalchemy >=1.4,<2 due to https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/57049. To avoid this warning upgrade to sqlalchemy 2.x")
```

I’d like to work on a fix.
This was fixed for Series/DataFrame in https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/24581, while pandas has little support for masked arrays I think it makes sense to have `pd.array` support as well.

Implementation and tests are done (#63887). Please review when you have time.

## Context

pd.array(np.ma.array(..., mask=...)) was ignoring the mask, so masked entries were kept as raw values instead of NA.

## Implementation
In array() in construction.py, when data is a ma.MaskedArray, we convert it to a list with NA at masked positions and pass that through the existing dtype inference/construction path; when there is no mask we use np.asarray(data) as before.

It is not great behaviour, but it is currently the "expected" behaviour, I think. 

First, the FutureWarning you see comes from numpy (and returning this scalar False value), and as you can see this warning is no longer present when using a recent numpy versions. Then, it actually _does_ an element-wise comparison, or at least it attempts to do so, but one of the individual comparisons is raising an error (the error you see).

This comes from the fact that `pd.NA` (in contrast to None or np.nan) currently 1) propagates in comparisons (instead of returning True/False), and 2) has an ambiguous "boolean" value (i.e. `bool(pd.NA)` is not well defined and this raises an error):

The comparisons:
```python
>>> pd.NA == "a"
<NA>
>>> pd.NA == pd.NA
<NA>
>>> np.nan == "a"
False
>>> np.nan == np.nan
False
>>> None == "a"
False
>>> None == None
True
```

The value in a boolean context:
```python
>>> bool(pd.NA)
...
TypeError: boolean value of NA is ambiguous
>>> bool(np.nan)
True
>>> bool(None)
False
```

So what happens if you compare element-wise two numpy object-dtype arrays with strings and pd.NA, is that one of the individual comparisons involving pd.NA returns pd.NA, and then afterwards numpy tries to cast the result of the comparisons to a bool dtype (because numpy expects to return bool dtype for comparisons), and at that point `bool(pd.NA)` raises the error.

The workaround is to be explicit about which value to use for pd.NA when converting to numpy. Essentially what you did by replacing the NA values with None, or you could also do `str_arr.to_numpy(na_value=None)` instead of `np.asarray(str_arr)` and manually replacing.

My best guess is that ideally, the code that maps a (tuple of) key(s) to one or more positions _and_ the code that determines what will the new index be should all be ``MultiIndex`` or ``_LocationIndexer`` (not ``Series`` or ``DataFrame``) code.

I like to have "pandas data types" with a consistent interface:

For example, for datetime-like data, we currently have:

```python

# vs
ser.astype("timestamp[us][pyarrow]")

# How to specify a "datetime" dtype being agnostic about the exact backend you are using?
# -> should use a single name and will pick the default backend based on your settings
ser.astype(pd.datetime("ns"))
# or
ser.astype(pd.timestamp("ns"))
# for user that want's to be explicit
ser.astype(pd.datetime("ns", backend=".."))
```

Another example, we currently have `pd.ArrowDtype("date64")` or `"date64[pyarrow]"`, but if we want to enable a date dtype by default, users shouldn't need to know this is stored using pyarrow under the hood, so this could be `pd.date()` or `"date"`?

---

**Logical data types** vs physical data types:

* For the "string" data type, we can store that with python objects or pyarrow strings (and now potentially also numpy's new string dtype), and then further for pyarrow, there are still 5 physical data types that all represent strings: string, large_string, string_view, dictionary[string], run_length_encoded[string] -> they all hold "logical" string values

For pandas, I think most users should care about logical data types, and not too much about the physical data type (and we can choose the best default, and advanced users can give hints which to use for performance optimizations)

---

Assuming we want a single pandas interface to all dtypes, we need to decide:

- how to let users construct them: functional (`pd.string()` vs class constructors (`pd.StringDtype()`)
- how to structure the DType classes: single class per logical type that are "backend-parametrized" (eg `pd.StringDtype(backend="arrow")`, `pd.StringDtype(backend="numpy")`) or separate classes based on the physical storage (what we have right now with eg `pd.Int64Dtype()` and `pd.ArrowDtype(pa.int64())`)

I think we already have both types somewhat, so we will need to clean this up to a certain extent whichever choice we make: 

- `pd.StringDtype(backend="python|"pyarrow")` is an example of using a single dtype class (that users can instantiate) as an interface to multiple implementations of the actual memory/compute (i.e. in this case we actually have multiple ExtensionArray classes that map to this single dtype depending on the backend)  
  (although I know we also have `pd.ArrowDtype(pa.string())` which then uses a different DType class) 
- `np.dtype("int64")` / `pd.Int64Dtype()` / `pd.ArrowDtype(pa.int64())` is essentially an example of a logical integer type where the entry point is a different class depending on which implementation you want (I know this wasn't necessarily designed together /grown historically, and I am mixing with also numpy dtypes, but it _is_ the current situation as how users face it)  
  While we could decide to have a single `pd.Int64Dtype(backend="numpy"|"pyarrow")` parametrized class (mimicking the string case above), or we could also decide that we are fine with having both `pd.Int64Dtype` (numpy based) and `pd.ArrowDtype` classes, but then I think we would need another entry point for users like `pd.int64()` factory function that can then create an instance of either of those classes (depending on your settings, or depending on a keyword you pass)

So while those class constructors indeed already exist, I think we have to repurpose or change the existing ones (and add new ones) to some extent anyway. And it is also not because we have those classes right now, that we can't decide we want to hide them more from the user by providing an alternative. I don't think there are already that many users that use `pd.Int64Dtype()` directly, and (_if we would prefer that interface_) there is certainly still room to start pushing a functional constructor interface.

@rhshadrach

I looked into this. It seems the C-tokenizer is aggressively sniffing and skipping BOM bytes before the codec layer even gets them.

To fix this without breaking backward compatibility (like for Excel files), I propose a tri-state logic in the wrapper that passes a flag down to the C-engine:

1. encoding=None (Default): Strip BOM (Keeps current "helpful" behavior for existing users).

2. encoding='utf-8-sig': Strip BOM (Explicit user intent).

3. encoding='utf-8': Preserve BOM (Fixes the bug, aligns with Python standard).

Basically, this ensures read_csv("excel.csv") keeps working cleanly, but read_csv("...", encoding="utf-8") strictly respects the bytes.

Plan is to plumb a strip_bom flag from CParserWrapper down to tokenizer.c. Does this sound right to you?

> 1. encoding=None (Default): Strip BOM (Keeps current "helpful" behavior for existing users).

This seems to me to be equivalent to a default of `utf-8-sig`. I agree with having this as a default. In addition, we can deprecate the current behavior for `utf-8` where users will only see a deprecation warning if they are specifying `encoding="utf-8"` and the file has a BOM.

Thanks @zkurtz for notifying me in the repository. And hello @WillAyd, I'm the current universal-pathlib maintainer.

> what does upath offer that isn't covered by that

There are two reasons for using universal-pathlib instead of fsspec directly, and both are basically convenience features.
1. A UPath instance combines the path string (fsspec uri) and the storage_options mapping in one container.
2. universal-pathlib users usually prefer the pathlib interface to construct paths (uris)

The current feature request basically asks for simplifying the following pattern:


```python
from upath import UPath
import pandas as pd

pth = UPath("s3://bucket/file.csv", some_option=True, other_option=123)

pd.DataFrame({"A": [1, 2, 3]}).to_csv(pth.as_uri(), storage_options=pth.storage_options)
pd.read_csv(pth.as_uri(), storage_options=pth.storage_options)

```

Currently, I would recommend against directly depending on `universal-pathlib` and against adding direct support for `UPath` instances via checking for the `UPath` interface.

For historic reasons, all `UPath` subclasses incorrectly pretend to be a local Path (they implement `__fspath__`, which makes them `os.PathLike`). In a future Python version a `pathlib.PathBase` class for concrete (virtual) Paths should become available and will be the correct subclass to test for in `pandas.io.common._get_filepath_or_buffer`. Once `UPath` will inherit from `pathlib.PathBase` (or a backport of `PathBase`) the logic in `_get_filepath_or_buffer` can be tweaked so that when `filepath_or_buffer` is detected as a `pathlib.PathBase` subclass, a buffer instance can be created by calling `filepath_or_buffer.open(mode=mode, encoding=encoding)`.

This refactor in `universal-pathlib` is tracked here fsspec/universal_pathlib#193 and work on `pathlib.PathBase` is ongoing in cpython.

As soon as the refactor in `universal-pathlib` is completed, I would be happy to contribute a PR to have a concrete example for discussion.

Cheers,

It appears that the issue relates to `_generate_cython_apply_func` in `pandas/core/window/rolling.py` (inside `RollingAndExpandingMixin`). It seems that while `groupby` reorders the values, `self._on` retains the original order, causing the mismatch.

I tried aligning the index as follows, and it seems to resolve the issue. Here is the diff of the potential fix:

```diff
# pandas/core/window/rolling.py

     def _generate_cython_apply_func(
         self,
         args: tuple[Any, ...],
         kwargs: dict[str, Any],
         raw: bool | np.bool_,
         function: Callable[..., Any],
     ) -> Callable[[np.ndarray, np.ndarray, np.ndarray, int], np.ndarray]:
         from pandas import Series
 
         window_func = partial(
             window_aggregations.roll_apply,
             args=args,
             kwargs=kwargs,
             raw=bool(raw),
             function=function,
         )
 
+        apply_index = self._on
+        if not raw and isinstance(self, BaseWindowGroupby):
+            # Groupby rolling reorders values by group; align the index to match.
+            groupby_indices = list(self._grouper.indices.values())
+            if groupby_indices:
+                groupby_order = np.concatenate(groupby_indices)
+                apply_index = self._on.take(groupby_order)
+            else:
+                apply_index = self._on[:0]

         def apply_func(values, begin, end, min_periods, raw=raw):
             if not raw:
                 # GH 45912
-                values = Series(values, index=self._on, copy=False)
+                values = Series(values, index=apply_index, copy=False)
             return window_func(values, begin, end, min_periods)
 
         return apply_func
```

@Moriyuki-S thanks for the excellent investigation! You correctly identified the root cause in `_generate_cython_apply_func`.

I have concerns about relying on `indices.values()` order. As you mentioned, `groupby(sort=True)` (the default) processes groups in sorted order, but `indices.values()` follows dictionary insertion order. 

For example, if your data has `Id=2` before `Id=1`:
- `indices.values()` yields: `[[Id=2 indices], [Id=1 indices]]` (insertion order)
- But `rolling` processes: `[Id=1 values, Id=2 values]` (sorted order)

This would cause a new misalignment.

I've been working on a fix that aligns with `self._grouper.result_index` to handle the sort order correctly. 

Either way, your diagnosis was spot-on and saved a lot of debugging time. 🙌

Was the idea that _if_ the ufunc returns a `str`-ish dtype, that it's re-wrapped in `StringArray`?

> Why isn't the dtype of the output just whatever the ufunc returns?

Just because of how it is implemented at the moment. For the python-backed StringArray, it currently gets its `__array_ufunc__` from the NumpyExtensionArray base class, which at

https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/ef4a9c3f6cbb53dc1d95e85a09e356f399355be2/pandas/core/arrays/numpy_.py#L186

essentially does (for the simple cases of returning 1 array as result):

```python
    def __array_ufunc__(self, ufunc: np.ufunc, method: str, *inputs, **kwargs):
        ...

        result = getattr(ufunc, method)(*inputs, **kwargs)
        return type(self)(result)
```

And so for the StringArray subclass, it uses the `StringArray(..)` constructor for wrapping the result. It's at that point that we should do inference instead.

For the pyarrow-backed string array, this uses the `__array_ufunc__` of the base ExtensionArray class, which through the `default_array_ufunc()` helper function essentially does:

```python
    def __array_ufunc__(self, ufunc: np.ufunc, method: str, *inputs, **kwargs):
        ...

        return getattr(ufunc, method)(*inputs, **kwargs)
```

i.e. just returning the numpy array result from the numpy ufunc, instead of wrapping it again in a pandas array.

For both cases, we should have some logic of wrapping the numpy array into an appropriate pandas ExtensionArray, if possible (and "appropriate" will then also depend on exactly which ExtensionArray is being used ..)

Methods such as `sum` can be used by wrapping the array in a Series.

```python
arr = pd.array(["a"], dtype="string[pyarrow]")
print(Series(arr == arr).sum())
# 1
```

These methods are only implemented at the array level on an as-needed basis.
Why? Series have an `.index`, which complicates semantics, e.g. a RangeIndex becomes a integer index when slicing and allocates the integers, whereas an array just has positional indices.

This seems to be specifically an issue in `align` when the other operand is a DataFrame instead of a series

```python
>>> ser1 = pd.Series(index=["a", "b"])
>>> ser2 = pd.Series(index=range(3))
>>> res1, res2 = ser1.align(ser2, join="left")
>>> res1.index
Index(['a', 'b'], dtype='str')
>>> res1, res2 = ser1.align(pd.DataFrame({0: ser2}), join="left")
>>> res1.index
Index(['a', 'b'], dtype='object')
```

And the align behaviour boils down to:

```python
>>> idx_str = pd.Index(["a", "b"], dtype=str)
>>> idx_obj = pd.Index(["a", "b"], dtype=object)
>>> 
>>> idx_str.join(idx_obj, how="left")
Index(['a', 'b'], dtype='object')
```

So the question here is whether this is actually the expected behaviour. In doing `res = s.str.cat(pd.Series(["A", "B", "C"]), sep=",", na_rep="-")`, you are passing a Series with an integer range index to `cat()`. At that point we have an operation between an object with str index vs integer range index. The common dtype for those is `object` dtype. In that sense, this is the expected behaviour.

However, since this is doing a "left" index join, one could expect that it is doing a bit more work to preserve the left index' dtype if there is no overlap. At the moment we don't special case such a left join without overlap, though. For example also an integer index gets cast to object:

```python
>>> pd.Index([1, 2, 3])
Index([1, 2, 3], dtype='int64')
>>> pd.Index([1, 2, 3]).join(pd.Index(["a", "b"]))
Index([1, 2, 3], dtype='object')
```
Closely related: https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/62949

I've opened PR #63485 to fix this issue.

The root cause was `Index.join()` losing StringDtype on left joins when there's no overlap with the other index. The fix preserves StringDtype when:
- Join method is "left"
- Left index has StringDtype  
- Right index does NOT have StringDtype
- No overlap exists (join result equals left index)

This minimal change ensures `str.cat(Series)` now preserves the StringDtype index as expected, while maintaining backward compatibility for cases with actual overlap.

Looking at this in more detail, I'm no longer so certain on my previous comment. I was thinking of `Series.str.cat` as a transform, but even with `how="left"` this need not be the case. It will only be the case there when the join is 1-to-{0,1}, and not 1-to-many. We could still guarantee preservation of the caller's index in such a narrow case, but I feel this makes predicting the behavior of the method itself difficult. Having the rule "the index dtype will be the common dtypes of the two indices joined" always apply is much simpler.

The behavior of `Index.join` in question here also occurs with `DataFrame.join` (and hence, `DataFrame.merge`), and I don't think we'd want these to diverge. I'm now leaning toward having no change here.

> Did something change here

The default image used to build the wheel from [pypa/cibuildwheel](https://github.com/pypa/cibuildwheel?tab=readme-ov-file) changed. Dropping support for `glibc<2.28` was a side effect.

cc @jorisvandenbossche @mroeschke

> Wondering if this shift in manylinux wheel support is an intentional change for this release and future versions?

It was not intentional in the sense that we (at least I) weren't aware that this change happened, but the tool we use for building wheels, cibuildwheel, intentionally changed their default manylinux build (https://cibuildwheel.pypa.io/en/stable/changelog/#v300), as @Alvaro-Kothe mentioned above.

And we updated the cibuildwheel version to be able to add Python 3.14 support, without considering the side effect of bumping the manylinux version (if not specifically updating the configuration to keep it).

It is unfortunate that this manylinux version bump happened in a bugfix release (and I am happy to consider a 2.3.4 release to add them back), but longer term (and for the next major release 3.0) I think we want to keep the change a bumped manylinux version. Especially given the fact that also numpy bumped their manylinux version a few months ago with their 2.3.0 release (https://numpy.org/doc/2.3/release/2.3.0-notes.html)

FWIW, I was curious why people run into compilation issues with pandas, and not already with numpy which would need to be installed before compiling pandas, and so which also bumped the manylinux version. But I assume this is because numpy 2.3 also does not support Python 3.9 (or 3.10), thus when installing pandas on 3.9, you will get an older numpy version which also still has the older manylinux wheels.

Quick thoughts:

> Do we add a reso-like keyword to the constructors? Or use/respect "unit"?

My gut is saying this should use/respect "unit" as it's not clear to me how "unit" and a reso-like keyword would cooperate?

> With non-nano np.timedelta64 objects that don't overflow when cast to nano, do we still cast?

Based on the GH issues I remember seeing in the past, generally people were hoping `datetime64[s]` was not cast to `datetime64[ns]` for example, but this behavior has been around for a while and some users may have gotten use to it. I would _think_ this would be a welcome change as the "old" behavior could be preserved with `astype("...64[ns]")`?

> Similar with pytimedelta...

Under the assumption `unit : str, default 'ns'` is still the default after this feature, I would expect `"ns"` for the current non-raising cases

Do keep in mind I don't have much experience using the date functionality even as-is.

> Do we add a reso-like keyword to the constructors? Or use/respect "unit"?

For the "use/respect unit" option, I think this would mean that a user specifying `pd.Timedelta(1, unit='days')` would always have a resolution of days. Is there a downside to this? One thought is combining different units (and hence, resolutions) would constantly require conversions. But maybe different resolutions would be cached under the hood.

Another option, if being able to specify the resolution is advantageous, would be to allow units such as `days[s]` or `days[ns]` etc. Unspecified could then default to ns.

> `pd.Timedelta(timedelta(days=106752))` currently raises, in the future will presumably come back with a 'us' reso.

Is this value-dependent behavior? If everything "just works", then I don't have much of a concern. However, if getting back one resolution vs another can cause odd results in edge cases, this could be surprising and lead to hard to find bugs. If that is the case, I would lean toward raising and making the user specify the resolution.

> For the "use/respect unit" option, I think this would mean that a user specifying pd.Timedelta(1, unit='days') would always have a resolution of days. Is there a downside to this?

Not really, just an API change.

> One thought is combining different units (and hence, resolutions) would constantly require conversions.

Yah, I've handled comparisons between scalars of different resolutions, but addition/subtraction (and division for Timedelta) it's not obvious what the right behavior is (i think numpy silently converts in ways that sometimes overflow, have examples/tests written down somewhere).  I think we provide an .astype-like API to allow conversion and otherwise raise on potentially-ambiguous operations.

> * Do we add a reso-like keyword to the constructors?  Or use/respect "unit"?

The existing keyword is about *"how to interpret the user input"*, and what we now want is *"how to store the parsed value"*. Those two are not necessarily the same, and I personally don't think we can simply assume they are (e.g. I think it would be quite common use case that you want to convert values that represent for example hours, but you want to store then in microseconds for compatibility with other data). 

In addition, we allow more units here for this keyword than what I would implement as possible resolution of the _dtype_. 
But given the responses above, we should maybe have this discussion explicitly about which resolutions we want to support. For example, about:

> For the "use/respect unit" option, I think this would mean that a user specifying pd.Timedelta(1, unit='days') would always have a resolution of days. Is there a downside to this?

My answer would be: we don't support a resolution of days, so such a resulting value is simply not possible (and thus it would be impossible to always respect the `unit` from the constructor.

(it's certainly unfortunate, though, that the `unit` keyword is not directly available for specifying the resulting storage unit .., as that would be the logical keyword name for this)


> * Similar with pytimedelta.  `pd.Timedelta(timedelta(days=106752))` currently raises, in the future will presumably come back with a 'us' reso.  So what about currently non-raising cases like `pd.Timedelta(timedelta(days=106751))`?  Does it stay ns or become us?

I think long term, the logical behaviour would be that any `datetime.timedelta` conversion by default results in "us" (since that is the "native" resolution of datetime.timedelta), regardless of the actual value. 
That will be a breaking change though, and I suppose we can only make that at some point in a major release (eg when also changing the default resolution), and on the short term keep using "ns" for this (and thus value-dependent behaviour).

```
            a) add a keyword e.g. "reso", e.g.

                In [4]: pd.Timestamp(4567, unit="us", reso="us")

            b) repurpose the "unit" keyword to specify the output resolution, e.g.

                In [4]: pd.Timestamp(4567, unit="us")

            The main place where this would cause an issue is if the user wants a different input resolution vs output resolution, in which case we would direct the user to convert post-construction along the lines of:

                In [5]: pd.Timestamp(4567, unit="s").as_unit("us")

            (ATM there is a private _as_unit which will likely be made public)

            c) don't specify it, infer it from the input, let users convert post-construction if they want.

            If we were starting fresh, b) would be my preferred API.  Backwards-compat concerns make a) more appealing. If we want to provide something user-facing in 1.5, a) seems like the only option.

        - Resolution Inference - scalars
            - np.datetime64, np.timedelta64 have natural resolutions attached to them. We should preserve these wherever possible and cast to the nearest support resolution otherwise.  e.g. Timestamp(np.datetime64(4, "ms")) would retain millisecond resolution.
            - pydatetime and pytimedelta objects naturally have microsecond resolution. The Timestamp/Timedelta constructors should preserve these.
            - strings are the harder case.  Should e.g. `Timestamp("2022-06-20 08:21:04")` come back with second-resolution?  I lean towards "yes".

        - Resolution Inference - arrays
            If we do inference on scalars, presumably we would want the analogous inference on arrays of scalars. This raises questions about what to do with mixed-resolution inputs:

                In [3]: pd.to_datetime(["2016-01-02 03:04:05", "2016-06-07 08:09:10.111", "2017-11-20 12:13:14:156789"])


    - Arithmetic between Timestamps/Timedelta of mismatched resolution?
        - Options:
            a) Raise in all cases
                We currently do this for division (truediv, rtruediv, floordiv, rfloordiv) on Timedelta
            b) Cast to the higher resolution like numpy:

                In [2]: td = np.timedelta64(1, "h")
                In [3]: dt = np.datetime64("1994-01-02 03:04:05")
                In [4]: dt + td
                Out[4]: numpy.datetime64('1994-01-02T04:04:05')

                In [5]: td + dt
                Out[5]: numpy.datetime64('1994-01-02T04:04:05')

            c) Cast to the lower resolution
            d) (the current choice) Cast to the lower resolution *if* doing so is lossless

                In [3]: ts = pd.Timestamp("2016-01-01 02:03:04")._as_unit("s")
                In [4]: other = pd.Timestamp(500_000_000)._as_unit("ms")

                In [5]: ts - other
                [...]
                ValueError: Timestamp subtraction with mismatched resolutions is not allowed when casting to the lower resolution would require lossy rounding.

                i) ATM (2022-06-20 16:01 UTC) this check is in place for Timestamp.__sub__(datetimelike) but not for Timedelta. The intention is to implement it for all the relevant add/sub ts/td combinations.
                ii) ATM (2022-06-19 16:01 UTC) this check is not implemented for DatetimeArray or TimedeltaArray.
            
                iii) The main reason for choosing d) over a) is that a) would break user code if/when, as expected, we change constructor behavior for Timestamp(pydatetime_object) to have microsecond resolution, e.g:
```

The issue appears to be one of violated assumptions:

The `take` function from `_mixins.py` assumes that the output of its call to `take` from `algorithms.py` has the same dtype as the `NDArrayBackedExtensionArray` object that the _mixins `take` is originally called on. This is not always the case, since `algorithms.take` promotes integer types to floating-point types to accommodate NaN values when they occur.

Location of the bug (in _mixins.py, line 176):
```python
        new_data = take(
            self._ndarray,
            indices,
            allow_fill=allow_fill,
            fill_value=fill_value,
            axis=axis,
        )
        return self._from_backing_data(new_data)
```

I propose setting `_ndarray.dtype` on `self` (of type `NDArrayBackedExtensionArray`) to the dtype of the output `new_data` of the sub-call to `take` before assigning the array data from `new_data` to `self` and returning.

This would ensure that the dtypes match between `self` and `new_data` in all cases and ultimately that the dtype reported by `self` is accurate.

I think Copy on Write only applies to different pandas objects that share the same data.

Here ``df.index is s.index``, so it shouldn't apply since they are the same object. 

We could fix this issue by creating a new Index object sharing values with the original index when you index into the DF, but I don't think that's the way to go.

I'll leave this open for others to comment.

EDIT: Typo

> Here df.index == s.index, so it shouldn't apply since they are the same object.

Isn't that the problem Copy-on-Write is solving though? It wasn't obvious when objects were views and when they weren't. IMO it's not at all intuitive that these are the same object when the objects these indexes belong to are no longer views on the same data.

I personally wouldn't change the fact that you can mutate an Series/DataFrame object's index/columns attributes (for example, that would also mean that `df.index.names = ...` would stop working, and that would be a quite big breaking change, and also just a behaviour that is good to keep IMO).

But when you create a _new_ object, like creating a Series from a DataFrame column, at that point I think we should consider also not propagating mutable state of the indexes between both (independent) objects.




> Here `df.index is s.index`, so it shouldn't apply since they are the same object.

Yes, it is correct that they are currently "identical", which explains why we see propagation of mutating their attributes.

> It wasn't obvious when objects were views and when they weren't. IMO it's not at all intuitive that these are the same object when the objects these indexes belong to are no longer views on the same data.

Yes, now that we generally create new objects from indexing operations (eg also getting the same column twice doesn't give identical objects, i.e. `df["col"] is df["col"]` gives False), I would personally also expect that their indices are no longer identical / shared. Of course under the hood we still share the data, but just by each time creating a shallow copy.

I propose a more gradual approach to meson (merge #49115).

1. switch to nonvendor versioneer #49924. 
2. move project metadata to pyproject.toml #49917
3. enable PEP 517 using setuptools; make all necessary changes to CI and doc. 
4. merge all meson build scripts, and add a separate CI job to test meson.

At this point, almost everything in #49115 would be included. Then we could wait for the editable wheel and all the other necessary features/fixes on meson. When everyone is satisfied, we then modify the backend setting in pyproject.toml to make the final switch.

I would not go forward with setuptools PEP 517, since it's just going to get replaced by meson, and you can't have two build systems in pyproject.toml.

The reason it is safe to modify the backend setting in pyproject.toml now, is because that it doesn't break people with editable installs(pip is smart enough to fall back to setup.py develop).

> At this point, almost everything in #49115 would be included. Then we could wait for the editable wheel and all the other necessary features/fixes on meson. When everyone is satisfied, we then modify the backend setting in pyproject.toml to make the final switch.

The problem is that meson builds won't work until the build backend is set to pyproject.toml. I would also really not prefer waiting. It is *really* hard to keep the meson PR open and up to date, and even if you can't really use meson locally without the editable installs, I think the reduction in CI time is well worth it.

```python
cython_args = ['--include-dir', meson.current_build_dir()]

endif
```

It supports random state, but not much else yet. I would like some feedback on the approach and the overall feature from the maintainers before continuing with this feature.  I haven't included edge case handling yet, but the idea I think is as .sample() - raise a ValueError is n exceeds length of object.

```Python
def sample_window(
            self,
            n: int | None = None,
            axis: Axis | None = None,
            random_state: RandomState | None = None,
    ) -> Self:
        """
        Return a contiguous window of items from the object. The startint point of the window is randomly selected.

        Selects a random index and will return the next `n` items in the axis.

        You can use `random_state` for reproducibility.

        Parameters
        ----------
        n : int, optional
            Number of items from axis to return in the window.
            Default = 1
        random_state : int, array-like, BitGenerator, np.random.RandomState, np.random.Generator, optional
            If int, array-like, or BitGenerator, seed for random number generator.
            If np.random.RandomState or np.random.Generator, use as given.
            Default ``None`` results in sampling with the current state of np.random.
        axis : {0 or 'index', 1 or 'columns', None}, default None
            Axis to sample. Accepts axis number or name. Default is stat axis
            for given data type. For `Series` this parameter is unused and defaults to `None`.

        Returns
        -------
        Series or DataFrame
            A new object of same type as caller containing a contiguous window `n` items
            randomly from the caller object.

        Notes
        -----

        To ensure the window can be sampled we sample the random index from the range [0, len(axis) - n].

        Examples
        --------
        >>> df = pd.DataFrame(
        ...     {
        ...         "num_legs": [2, 4, 8, 0],
        ...         "num_wings": [2, 0, 0, 0],
        ...         "num_specimen_seen": [10, 2, 1, 8],
        ...     },
        ...     index=["falcon", "dog", "spider", "fish"],
        ... )
        >>> df
                num_legs  num_wings  num_specimen_seen
        falcon         2          2                 10
        dog            4          0                  2
        spider         8          0                  1
        fish           0          0                  8

        Sample a contiguous window of size 2. Note that we use `random_state`
        to ensure the reproducibility of the examples.

        >>> df.sample_window(2, random_state=1)
                num_legs  num_wings  num_specimen_seen
        dog            4          0                  2
        spider         8          0                  1

        """
        if axis is None:
            axis = 0

        axis = self._get_axis_number(axis)
        obj_len = self.shape[axis]

        # Process random_state argument
        rs = common.random_state(random_state)

        valid_range = obj_len - n

        print(f"obj_len: {obj_len} n: {n} valid_range: {valid_range}")

        # User defines what size window they want then function will take random sample from which the next N is valid for that size
        # e.g. if n = 10, len(df) == 100, then sample from 0-90
        sampled_index = rs.randint(0, valid_range + 1)  # sample.sample(valid_range, 1, False, None, rs).item()

        # Sampled indices has to be a list of valid indices
        sampled_indices = [sampled_index + i for i in range(n)]

        print(f"Sampled index: {sampled_index} - sampled_indices: {sampled_indices}")

        result = self.take(sampled_indices, axis=axis)

        return result
```

I spent some time trying to reproduce this locally and wanted to share what I found.

I couldn’t reproduce the precision loss on my setup. I tested with SQL Server 2022 (Docker), ODBC Driver 17 for SQL Server, pyodbc 5.3.0, and pandas 3.0.0rc1. Even with fast_executemany=True, both regular tables and local temp tables (#tables) preserved full DATETIME2 precision.

Digging a bit deeper, this seems consistent with a known limitation in the ODBC/pyodbc layer when fast_executemany is used with local temp tables. In that mode the driver relies on sp_describe_undeclared_parameters for type inference, and that stored procedure doesn’t work with #temp tables. When that happens, the driver can fall back to weaker type handling, which can truncate datetime precision. This is documented in pyodbc#295 and the pyodbc wiki.See https://github.com/mkleehammer/pyodbc/issues/295 for more details.


What’s interesting is that this doesn’t seem to happen with newer drivers / newer SQL Server, which makes me think this is environment- or configuration-specific (possibly Azure SQL Database or older driver versions), rather than something pandas is doing wrong.

One workaround that’s often suggested upstream is adding UseFMTONLY=Yes to the connection string, which forces the driver to use SET FMTONLY instead of sp_describe_undeclared_parameters. Other workarounds are also listed in the pyodbc docs.

Given that I can’t reproduce this on a recent setup, this might be best handled via documentation and guidance rather than a pandas-side code change.
