> ```
> 
> An important highlight of this example is the ability to reference the grouped value -- eg, `x['key']` -- inside the applied function.
> 
> pandas also supports grouping on arbitrary mapping functions, iterables, and lots of other objects. In these cases, the grouped value is not represented as a named column in the DataFrame. Thus, when using apply(...), there is no apparent way to access the group key value. The only alternative is to use a (slow) for-loop solution as in:

> foo = lambda _k, _g: ...
> grouped = df.groupby(grouper)
> result_iter = (foo(key, group) for key, group in grouped) 
> key_iter = (key for key, group in grouped)
> pd.DataFrame.from_records(result_iter, index=key_iter)
> ```
> 
> IMHO, the ability to access the grouped value in an idiomatic way from within the applied function is ergonomically important; the groupby-apply idiom is at best partially realized without it.

However I'd hazard a guess that you'd still have a bad time using an object that pandas recognizes as iterable by the presence of an `__iter__` method even though it is not. Ideally it does seem to me that pandas should be implementing try-except to determine whether an object is iterable. CPython's quirk of checking for `__getitem__` (the reason that `TypedUnits` defines `__iter__`) demonstrates this.

```python

    def __init__(self, values):
        self._values = values

    def __getitem__(self, key):
        return self._values[key]

print(iter(mylist))
# <iterator object at 0x743ed844dd50>
```

Upon some investigation, I found out that the bug might be in the following function:
https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/bd5ed2f6e2ef8713567b5c731a00e74d93caaf64/pandas/io/sql.py#L166

In version v1.5.x, the `_wrap_result` function directly wrapped list of dicts into a dataframe with the `from_records` function,
https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/2e218d10984e9919f0296931d92ea851c6a6faf5/pandas/io/sql.py#L146

But with version v2.0.0 it calls a newly added function, `_convert_arrays_to_dataframe` in the following line:
https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/bd5ed2f6e2ef8713567b5c731a00e74d93caaf64/pandas/io/sql.py#L176

This function uses `lib.to_object_array_tuples` function which according to its documentation does the following 
"Convert a list of tuples into an object array. Any subclass of tuple in `rows` will be casted to tuple."
https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/bd5ed2f6e2ef8713567b5c731a00e74d93caaf64/pandas/io/sql.py#L148

What it fails to consider is the data that this lib function receives might not be a *list of tuples* but instead it could be *list of dicts*. Therefore, it fails to return correct data when a list of dicts is passed to it that comes from the `cursor.fetchall()` here:
https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/bd5ed2f6e2ef8713567b5c731a00e74d93caaf64/pandas/io/sql.py#L2303

I am almost certain this occurs in the `SQLiteDatabase` class which is also a fallback when SQL Alchemy connector is missing. (for example, DBAPI2 connections with result sets as lists of dicts)

Let me know if this paints a correct picture because I have never done this before. I hope this helps. 🙂

Regarding border styles, the error in #30008 appears when a border color is defined but border style is not (or border style is none). The source of the error is in `pd.io.excel._XlsxStyler` where the style mapping `(("top", "style"), "top")` causes the prop dictionary to set `props["top"] = {"color": "#000000"}`. 

The root cause however is in `io.formats.excel` under `_border_style`. Whenever the function returns `None`, it should instead return `"none"` as a string. The reason for this is that `"none"` is a valid border style. When it is set to `None`, the style gets removed in `remove_none` during `build_xlstyle`, which leads to the TypeError.

In summary, I believe replacing each `return None` with `return "none"` in `_border_style` will fix the error. Alternatively, set `color` to `None` if the style is none in `build_border`.

Just for anyone who still want to style their table index, here is my solution: Note: This is a method which focuses on exporting your multi-index table as an excel with alternating colours for primal index, as long as it looks like what it is inside python, I dont care whether certain column in excel is really 'column' or 'index' inside python. First, do the routine: ``` from io import BytesIO from openpyxl import load_workbook filename = r'' wb = load_workbook(filename, read_only=False, keep_vba=False) writer = pd.ExcelWriter(filename, engine='openpyxl') ``` Divide your dataframe df into two parts - coloured half and blank half. I am using light blue for this example. ``` lightblue_primalindex=sorted(set([_[0] for _ in df.index]), key=[_[0] for _ in df.index].index)[::2] lightblue_index=[df.index.get_loc(i) for i in lightblue_primalindex] ``` Here is the tricky part. Reset your dataframe as single index but preserve the structure by filling NaN to extra primal index column, this way they will not show in the styled dataframe nor in the exported excel later. ``` y=df.reset_index() y.loc[y.duplicated(''),'']=np.nan ``` Then apply the colouring with style and we are golden. ``` lightblue_df=pd.concat([y[lightblue_index[i]] for i in range(len(lightblue_index))]) y.style.apply(lambda x: pd.Series(['background-color: lightblue' if i in list(lightblue_df.index) else '' for i in range(0, len(y))],index=y.index)).to_excel(writer, sheet_name='', startrow=0 , startcol=0, index=False) writer.save() ``` Then you will get one excel with table looking exactly the same as that in python. References: 1. [Style single-index dataframe using style.applymap](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/71563286/different-color-of-each-row-in-dataframe-based-on-data-in-column) 2. [Style multi-index dataframe using Styler.set_table_styles](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/59769161/python-color-pandas-dataframe-based-on-multiindex)

Another format that is lacking support is `datetime.time` and `Timedelta`.  A couple related issues:

- `ExcelWriter._value_with_fmt` accepts `datetime.timedelta` but formats it as "0" (single integer, so it will essentially as the number of days, rounded). This may work for some use cases, but it assumes a lot about the purpose for the user's timedeltas.
- `ExcelWriter._value_with_fmt` does not accept `datetime.time`, and instead converts it to a string (which seems to default to "%H:%M:%S")
- `maybe_convert_css_to_tuples` in `styler_render.py` uses `str.split(":")` to split between property name and value. This prevents users from passing something like `"number-format: hh:mm"` to the styler. Using `partition` or passing `max_split` would fix this.
- One possible workaround to the `maybe_convert_css_to_tuples` issue would be for the user to return a `CSSList` instead of a string. However, `Styler._update_ctx` calls `pd.isna(c)` which returns an array of booleans if passed a CSSList, instead of a scalar.

I can confirm this issue. It is a parity gap between the NumPy-backed DatetimeIndex and the PyArrow-backed Index.

### Analysis
When using dtype_backend='pyarrow', the result is a generic pd.Index wrapping an ArrowExtensionArray. Unlike pd.DatetimeIndex, this generic class does not yet delegate properties like .month or .year to the underlying array.

### Workaround
Access these properties explicitly via the .dt accessor:
``` python
# Use .dt for pyarrow-backed indexes
df.groupby(df.index.dt.month).some_col.describe()
```
I suggest exposing these datetime properties on pd.Index when the underlying dtype is an Arrow timestamp to match DatetimeIndex behavior.

In my mind, the value in a docstring `defaults to [value]` should be the value that the user will get when they do not specify the argument. As such, the docstring here and in https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/63191 to me is perfectly fine. But we've had a few reports of this nature, so want to get more eyes on this. cc @pandas-dev/pandas-core

In this case, the situation is a bit complex because the keyword is being deprecated:

- The default was `copy=True` for pandas < 3
- With pandas 3 (or 2.3 with CoW enabled), the `copy` keyword is ignored (and for that reason, the default in the signature was changed to `None` in 2.3) 
- With pandas 3, a deprecation warning is issued if the keyword is specified (hence the default in the signature of `no_default` to catch when the user specified it), and the doc was update to say "default False" (although that is also not entirely correct)

In practice, people do get "kind of" a copy, so personally I would just leave the dosctring as is for now. But as I mentioned in the closed PR https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/63149#issuecomment-3564701585, we should update the _explanation_ of the keyword in the docstring to be clearer about the current situation (since we now are 3.0, and it is not a future change)

But on the general topic, I agree we should document the behaviour people get when they don't specify anything. And so I think we should in practice never document something like `"defaults to lib.no_default"`

In 2.3, the signature on `DataFrame.astype()` that is in the docs has `copy=None`, but the docstring says `copy: bool, default True`

In the dev version (3.0), the signature on `DataFrame.astype()` that is in the docs has `copy=<no default>`, but the docstring says `copy: bool, default False`

IMHO, in the docs throughout, we should try to make the signature and docstring consistent.  Having said that, if there is no default (as in 3.0), then the docstring should say that the code behaves as if `False` was passed.

In `pandas-stubs`, we've had cases where the docs say `lib.no_default`, and then we peek into the code to figure out what the real default behavior is, if changing the default would help.

Note:  In `pandas-stubs`, we have a policy of removing any deprecated arguments/methods/functions/classes, whenever we get around to it. So once 3.0 is out the door, we'll work on making the stubs more compatible with 3.0, which means we would remove the `copy` argument from the stub for `DataFrame.astype()` to discourage its use, and force people to change their code right away (assuming they are using a type checker).

> In the dev version (3.0), the signature on `DataFrame.astype()` that is in the docs has `copy=<no default>`, but the docstring says `copy: bool, default False`
> 
> IMHO, in the docs throughout, we should try to make the signature and docstring consistent. Having said that, if there is no default (as in 3.0), then the docstring should say that the code behaves as if `False` was passed.

I do not view the first paragraph here as an inconsistency. The `default...` portion of the docstring tells the user what happens if they do not specify the argument. I see no value in having `defaults...` mean the literal value in the signature; that information is already available in the signature.

> The `default...` portion of the docstring tells the user what happens if they do not specify the argument.

Maybe we should use different language, in the case the signature and docstring are different.  E.g., "`copy: bool, default behavior is False`"

So adding the word "behavior" differentiates from the use of a default _value_ in the signature, and default _behavior_ in the docstring.
My only opposition to changing the language to something better is the code churn on updating all of our functions. My opinion is that there is nothing wrong with the status quo.

Hi @jbrockmendel @IzidoroBaltazar,

From the repro it looks like `read_sql_query(..., coerce_float=True)` is coercing `decimal.Decimal` to `float64`, which silently loses precision for large integral values (IDs beyond `2**53`). I was able to reproduce this with a small sqlite setup, and setting `coerce_float=False` avoids the precision loss.

Repro I used:

```python
import sqlite3
import pandas as pd
from decimal import Decimal

sqlite3.register_adapter(Decimal, lambda d: str(d))
sqlite3.register_converter("DECIMAL", lambda b: Decimal(b.decode()))
con = sqlite3.connect(":memory:", detect_types=sqlite3.PARSE_DECLTYPES)
con.execute("CREATE TABLE t (longID DECIMAL)")
con.execute("INSERT INTO t (longID) VALUES (?)", (Decimal("305184080441754059"),))
con.commit()

raw = con.execute("SELECT longID FROM t").fetchone()[0]
print("sqlite type:", type(raw), "value:", raw)

df = pd.read_sql("SELECT longID FROM t", con, coerce_float=True)

v = df.loc[0, "longID"]
print("pandas value:", v, "type:", type(v))
print("as int:", int(v)) 
```

With `coerce_float=True` the value rounds to `305184080441754048` (via float), while the DB value is `305184080441754059`. With `coerce_float=False` it stays exact. I can take a first pass at this by adding a small regression test and proposing a fix so `coerce_float=True` does not coerce large integral `Decimal` values to float when it would be lossy.

So essentially I think this is a simplified example of what you could do before:

```python
>>> df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, np.nan, 3], "b": [np.nan, 20, 30]})
>>> df["a"].update(df["b"])
>>> df
      a     b
0   1.0   NaN
1  20.0  20.0
2  30.0  30.0

```

With pandas 2.3, that gives a FutureWarning, with pandas 3.0 that gives a ChainedAssignmentError (warning, here can definitely still update the warning message)

So, what is the best alternative to achieve the same?

Richard mentioned the following, but this requires an intermediate variable (which I find a bit unfortunate):

```python
>>> df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, np.nan, 3], "b": [np.nan, 20, 30]})
>>> ser = df["a"]
>>> ser.update(df["b"])
>>> df["a"] = ser
>>> df
      a     b
0   1.0   NaN
1  20.0  20.0
2  30.0  30.0
```

To avoid that, you can call this method on the dataframe directly, however because that aligns the input df, you have to rename it first:

```python
>>> df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, np.nan, 3], "b": [np.nan, 20, 30]})
>>> df.update(df[["b"]].rename(columns={"b": "a"}))
>>> df
      a     b
0   1.0   NaN
1  20.0  20.0
2  30.0  30.0
```

or a bit simpler (I only thought about this wondering if this wouldn't make it simpler if we supported that. Turns out we do, because that is coerced to a dataframe):

```python
>>> df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, np.nan, 3], "b": [np.nan, 20, 30]})
>>> df.update({"a": df["b"]})
>>> df
      a     b
0   1.0   NaN
1  20.0  20.0
2  30.0  30.0
```

Seeing those examples, I agree it would be nice if `update()` would also return the updated result (now that the methods with an `inplace` keyword do so, should we do that here as well?)

This is a consequence of the order of checks we do in to_datetime.  Re-ordering the checks would cause different inconsistencies.  I don't think its possible to combine the format path (array_strptime) with the unit path (array_to_datetime) bc array_strptime casts ints/floats to string and tries to parse them with the format.

It would of course be an additional step with potential performance overhead, but we _could_ in theory first do an `infer_dtype` on the input, and if it are strings just take the `array_strptime` path regardless of `unit`? 
But, we also support mixed input, which would still give inconsistencies anyway, I suppose

ATM we use array_strptime if first_non_null(arr) is a string.  In most cases this will be the same as infer_dtype returning "string", but they would differ in cases with `[string, integer]`.

I think if we really want consistent behavior we need to deprecate the array_strptime casting of integers to strings, after which array_strptime and array_to_datetime can be merged.  xref #55663.

There is no easy solution, right now: the problem is with `datetime.datetime.__add__` (and not not with `pd.Timedelta.__add__`). 

See this example:
```
import datetime
import pandas as pd

dt = datetime.datetime(2015, 1, 1, 0)
delta_2 = pd.to_timedelta(pd.date_range('2015-01-01 00', '2015-01-01 01', freq="1h").freq)
assert isinstance(delta_2, datetime.timedelta)

print(dt.__add__(delta_2))  # 2015-01-01 00:00:00
print(delta_2.__add__(dt))  # 2015-01-01 01:00:00
```
So python stdlib `datetime.datetime.__add__` method will see that `delta_2` is a `datetime.timedelta` instance and assume that it behaves like `datetime.timedelta(seconds=3600)`, which is not true.

As a general comment, maybe `datetime.datetime.__add__` is a little too optimistic, since for efficiency it assumes that the `pytimedelta` struct holds a valid value, while of course it could also query the higher level property `pd.Timedelta.seconds`... 

By the way, there is a generale feature of Python that allows subclasses to override their ancestors’ operations, see the note at the end of <https://docs.python.org/3/reference/datamodel.html#emulating-numeric-types>.

In fact
```
delta_1 = datetime.timedelta(seconds=3600)
print(delta_1 + delta_2)  # 0 days 02:00:00
```
works as expected, because `delta_1 + delta_2` will call the reflected `delta_2.__radd__(delta_1)` first, even if  `delta_1.__add__(delta_2)` does not return `NotImplemented`

```
repr(delta_1 + delta_2)  # "Timedelta('0 days 02:00:00')"
repr(delta_1.__add__(delta_2))  # 'datetime.timedelta(seconds=3600)'
repr(delta_2.__radd__(delta_1))  # "Timedelta('0 days 02:00:00')"
```

So maybe a way forward is to convince the CPython developers that special code should be added to `datetime.datetime.__add__(x)` to check first for a reflected operator if `type(x)` is a subclass of `datetime.timedelta`... but I think that it is highly improbable that a fix will be accepted form the side of CPython.

From the side of pandas, the obvious solution would be to ensure that `issubclass(pandas._libs.tslibs.timedeltas.Timedelta, datetime.timedelta)` returns false, so that CPython is forced to use the reflected 
```
delta_2.__radd__(dt)  # Timestamp('2015-01-01 01:00:00')
```
which works as expected.

Bottom line: do not mix python `datetime.*` objects with pandas time objects, because they are largely incompatible, and could give raise to strange behaviour.

Pandas datetime arithmetic is guaranteed to work: it is mixed python and pandas arithmetic which is problematic. Simply put, the pytimedelta structure *could* overflow, so it is simply not initialised for resolutions grater than µs. Note that this structure is *not* needed for Pandas temporal arithmetic, but only to claim that `pd.Timedelta` is a `datetime.timedelta` subclass...

Here a comparison to numpy behaviour, which was the model for Pandas implementation.

```
>>> issubclass(np.timedelta64, datetime.timedelta)
False
>>> np.timedelta64(1, 'ns').astype(datetime.timedelta)
1
>>> np.timedelta64(1, 'ms').astype(datetime.timedelta)
datetime.timedelta(microseconds=1000)
>>> np.timedelta64(10**9*24*3600*1000-1, 'ms').astype(datetime.timedelta)
datetime.timedelta(days=999999999, seconds=86399, microseconds=999000)
>>> np.timedelta64(10**9*24*3600*1000, 'ms').astype(datetime.timedelta)
86400000000000000
```

Main takes:
- `np.timedelta64` **does not** claims to be a `datetime.timedelta` subclass
- when an explicit cast to `datetime.timedelta` is possible without resolution loss, overflow, underflow, a `datetime.timedelta` object is returned, otherwise ant `int` without resolution.

OK looking at the source code a piece of the puzzle falls into place:

* the checking of the allowed values is done by `pandas.core.generic._rename`
   * the check is done only if `errors == "raise"` (see #13473)
   * this checks for the whole index value tuple's existence, not the individual levels.

* the transforming of the index values is done by `pandas.core.indexes.base._transform_index`. 
   * this substitutes each *part* of the index value tuple on whichever level
       * unless `level` is not None, in which case only on that level)
   * this works fine if `errors != "raise"`.

So these are incompatible, and in the case where `errors == "raise"` you can't rename multi level indexes.
Either the checking should be fixed or the transforming should be changed.

The former is probably less problematic (even though it doesn't solve *my* problem[1]) as people will have used the rename-on-every-level behaviour without `errors == "raise"` and changing this would break stuff.

This would work for us and is the behavior we are using in our use case.  

For reference, the use case is a .csv that serves as a controlled vocabulary for defined terms in order to map between fields-values-UI display terms.  It needs to be centralized in a single file as the actual values/UI meanings are reviewed/maintained by SME vs. developers

The code in question creates a dict that splits this apart, and could potentially be handled with an if/then since within a given field things are either all numeric or all not. But the 'if this is numeric, make it numeric, and if not leave it as a string' is the intended behavior as currently written.

Current function in use:
```
def get_terms_dictionary(display_terms, api_field, api_value, display_col):
    '''from a dataframe with the table display information, create a dictionary by field to match the database
    value to a value for use in the UI '''
    try:
        display_terms_list = display_terms[api_field].unique() # List of fields with matching display terms

        # Create a dictionary using the field as the key, and the dataframe to map database values to display text as the value
        display_terms_dict = {}
        for i in display_terms_list:
            term_df = display_terms[display_terms.api_field == i]
            term_df = term_df[[api_value,display_col]]
            term_df = term_df.rename(columns={api_value: i, display_col: i + '_display'})
            term_df = term_df.apply(pd.to_numeric, errors='ignore')
            display_terms_dict[i] = term_df
        return display_terms_dict

    except Exception as e:
        traceback.print_exc()
        return None```

@deniskrds, do your proposed changes address this case as well?

Yes, the fix addresses this. As you observed, `union` already returns a new instance in this case, but `intersection` doesn't. The fix ensures both operations consistently return new Index instances (via shallow copy) rather than returning self. Since Index is immutable, sharing the underlying data is safe—what matters is you no longer get the same Python object. MultiIndex had the same issue, so the fix applies there as well. @warwickmm

The inconsistency is a bug IMO. I don't recall whether pandas should respect the read-only input during write operations and raise generally or deem it "surprising for users that they cannot write" and copy in this case

And this will happen for any Series where the underlying array is read-only, i.e. this is https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/62144

It is that with CoW this becomes more common. I had thought of `ser.values` in the issue, but going through `Index` is at the moment also a way to get this. 

IMO, as I argued in that issue, a setitem operation on a pandas Series or DataFrame object should essentially always work, and so I would consider that as a bug that we don't take into account the case of read-only arrays (you can also get that without CoW, like some corner cases with pyarrow).

But let's continue the discussion of that part in https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/62144 ?

---

That said, there is indeed another issue here. The inconsistency boils down to: `pd.Index(..)` has a `copy=False` default, while in `pd.Series()` we decided to copy by default if the input is an array (but use the CoW tracking for pandas Index/Series input). 

As a result, constructing the series directly does not give an underlying read-only array (it will copy the categorical or array):

```
>>> arr = np.array([0, 1])
... arr.flags.writeable = False
>>> ser = pd.Series(arr)
>>> ser[[False, True]] = 100
>>> ser
0      0
1    100
dtype: int64
```

While constructing the Series through a temporary Index causes the array to _not_ be copied, but the reference tracking is lost because the Index was only temporary.


So I would say that the inconsistency is caused by `Index` not copying the input data by default. We changed Series to copy array input by default when we introduced CoW. We should maybe do the same for `Index`?

Your example is not using the pyarrow "engine", but the "dtype backend". The engine is about which library to use to do the actual csv parsing, or the dtype backend is about which dtypes you want to use for the resulting dataframe. Both options are independent of each other (and you can in theory have all 4 combinations).

Using your example:

```python
>>> df = pd.read_csv(io.StringIO(data))  # by default will typically use `engine="c"`
>>> df.dtypes
name      str
age     int64
dtype: object
>>> df = pd.read_csv(io.StringIO(data), engine="pyarrow")
>>> df.dtypes
name      str
age     int64
dtype: object
>>> df = pd.read_csv(io.StringIO(data), dtype_backend="pyarrow")  # use the default c engine, but return ArrowDtypes
>>> df.dtypes
name    string[pyarrow]
age      int64[pyarrow]
dtype: object
>>> df = pd.read_csv(io.StringIO(data), engine="pyarrow", dtype_backend="pyarrow")

I am assuming that the following questions are about "with all those different variants, which string dtype should I use?"

> 1/what are the real impacts ?

The main choice you have to make is whether you want the default dtype (using np.nan as missing value indicator), or a "nullable" dtype using pd.NA. That choice has the biggest impact, because it determines some different missing value behaviour, it results in different result dtypes in various operations (eg getting the length of each string giving a series of default numpy int64 (or float64 if there are missing values) instead of a nullable Int64), etc. 

> 2/what's the fastest?

There is no black/white answer, but generally using "pyarrow" storage is (a lot) faster for element-wise `.str` operations, but can be slightly slower for other operations (joins, groupby). 
I did open https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/63105 as an issue to keep track of the fact that we should better document this.

(and then which of the string dtypes using pyarrow shouldn't matter that much)

> 3/what the old way that will be deprecated in a few years? What would be the target?

The "old" way being `object` dtype? 
Personally I don't think we are ever going to deprecate object dtype in general (as there are valid use cases for that), but we might at some point deprecate the ability to perform `.str.<..>` string operations through object dtype.

If you mean with the old way some of the StringDtype variants: the goal is to eventually reduce the number of variants (only support pd.NA and not np.nan as missing value indicator), but that is in the future and not yet really a concern right now, I would say (the string dtype with np.nan only becomes a default right now)

> 4/when you write "when PyArrow is installed.", isn't pyarrow installed with pandas? in what case wouldn't be?

No, pyarrow is not an actual hard requirement of pandas, so a plain `pip install pandas` without extras will not pull in pyarrow.

> 5/What are the impact on my code if I change nothing?

That's the goal of the [migration guide](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/user_guide/migration-3-strings.html) to explain: you will typically start to see `str` dtype instead of `object` dtype for columns with string data (unless you had `dtype='object` hardcoded), and so that might require some changes if your code relied explicitly on the fact that you had object dtype. The migration guide gives some examples of that (eg checking for the dtype). 
But all string operations will just keep working as they did before.

> What I have in mind is going with PyArrow storage with pd.NA values as the fastest/most modern solution but really not sure. I dream of a simpler solution with only one single representation of missing value and a single one string type. Refusing breaking changes is not always the solution.

I would personally say: if you are not really sure, just stick to the default (i.e. the string dtype using np.nan, not pd.NA), but make sure to install pyarrow as well, to ensure you use the "pyarrow" storage for the StringDtype.

We all dream of that simpler solution, I think ;), and the goal is to get there eventually. But there is more development needed for that. And to be clear, the current change in 3.0 to introduce a string dtype is already a breaking change.

We discussed this once more at the community dev meeting last week, how we can make the repr more informative, so one can actually _see_ the difference in dtype when inspecting data. 
The proposal to move forward here is to distinguish `__repr__` and `__str__` more (right now, they are largely the same for StringDtype).

`__str__` is generally used when showing the dtype when included in another representation, such as the dtype shown in the footer of a Series representation, or in the values when doing `df.dtypes`. `__repr__` is then typically used when actually interactively inspecting the dtype (e.g. checking `obj.dtype`, but not printing it), or eg used in error message of assert methods.

That has some balance in keeping the repr short in those DataFrame/Series representation, but having the full information available when actually looking at the dtype object itself.

The concrete proposal is then to keep `__str__` the same (this is currently `"str"` or `"string"` for NaN vs NA semantics). And to turn `__repr__` into a more verbose repr like `<StringDtype(storage='python', na_value=nan)>`.
(this brings it somewhat in line with Categorical dtype, where the str is `"category"` but the repr is a full `CategoricalDtype(..)` with categories and other attributes)

Generally the repr would then show all the arguments of the constructor, except that we were thinking we could omit defaults to make it a bit less verbose for those cases. In this case that would mean only show `storage='..'` if it is "python", i.e. (typically, if you have pyarrow installed) the opt-in variant. But for `na_value`, although this has a default, we would still show it always, given this has a much bigger impact on behaviour semantics.

> These implementation issues are not details and should not be hidden to the user (even the beginner).

This is indeed where we disagree .. I really think that beginners should almost _never_ have to think about those details, and ideally not even get exposed to those details. If there are common cases where they actually need to know right now, I think that is rather a sign that we need to fix or improve something, than that this newcomer should be aware of it. 
(for example, the memory overflow issues with pyarrow should simply not happen, that should be considered a bug we have to fix, and which I think is also more or less fixed at the moment because of always using the large string variant under the hood)

But anyway, I hope the proposal here is some compromise between not showing the dtype "details" constantly, while making it still very accessible (and shown by default when inspecting the dtype itself)

@Aokizy2 - unless I'm missing something, I think we just need to uncomment the two lines I highlighted in my last post, which I think is equivalent to what you proposed (and add tests). But this should not raise a performance warning.

@rhshadrach -Thanks for the direction. I've looked into the code, and I believe there's a small misunderstanding about those two commented lines.

The issue is that pc.add(key, pc.list_value_length(self._pa_array)) would produce an array of indices (one adjusted index for each list). However, the very next line pc.list_element(self._pa_array, key) requires its second argument (key) to be a single integer (scalar), not an array. This is exactly what the TODO comment itself states: “pyarrow does not allow element index to be an array.”

Therefore, simply uncommenting those two lines would result in a runtime ArrowNotImplementedError because we'd be passing an array where a scalar is expected.

To move forward, I think we have two options:

Option 1 (Workaround in Pandas): Implement the logic described in the comment, but handle the iteration ourselves (e.g., loop through each list, calculate the adjusted index, and extract the element). This would make .list[-1] work for users immediately.

Option 2 (Wait for upstream fix): Hold off on any workaround and focus on requesting or contributing the array-index feature directly in the PyArrow project. This would be the cleaner long-term solution.

I did some experimentation using the example provided.  Seems like using `groupby(axis=1)` is 3x faster:
```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

items = ["A_10", "A_20", "A_30", "B_10", "B_20", "B_30", "C_10", "C_20", "C_30"]

costs = np.random.default_rng().uniform(low=1, high=10_000, size=(1000, len(items)))

df = pd.DataFrame(costs, columns=items)

def grouper(c):
    if c.startswith("A"):
        return "ACCESS"
    if c.startswith("B"):
        return "BACKHAUL"
    if c.startswith("C"):
        return "CORE"

def transit(df):
    return (
        df.T.rename_axis(index=["colname"])
        .reset_index()
        .assign(group=lambda df: df["colname"].map(grouper))
        .drop(columns=["colname"])
        .groupby("group")
        .sum()
        .T
    )

def aggit(df):
    return df.groupby(by=grouper, axis=1).sum()
```

```python
%timeit transit(df)

2.96 ms ± 380 µs per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 100 loops each)

%timeit aggit(df)
931 µs ± 14.1 µs per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 1,000 loops each)
```

Inside that method, it seems we are explicitly doing the operation only on the _inner_ join of columns:

https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/311f92e2c68ef183c05d62be4d61a57ce1448c30/pandas/core/frame.py#L8450-L8456

and then afterwards just reindex the result. But so at that point, the dtypes of the original columns get completely ignored.

IIRC this used to be an outer-join and we operated on all columns, which I think would give the behavior the OP expects here.  I suspect that being more careful about what dtype to introduce when reindexing would also address #59529.  Using a void dtype might also be a good solution.

Vibe coded a solution for `frame.py/DataFrame`:

```python

    def _arith_method_with_reindex(self, right: DataFrame, op) -> DataFrame:
        """
        For DataFrame-with-DataFrame operations that require reindexing,
        operate only on shared columns, then reindex.

        Parameters
        ----------
        right : DataFrame
        op : binary operator

        Returns
        -------
        DataFrame
        """
        left = self

        # GH#31623, only operate on shared columns
        cols, lcol_indexer, rcol_indexer = left.columns.join(
            right.columns, how="inner", return_indexers=True
        )

        new_left = left if lcol_indexer is None else left.iloc[:, lcol_indexer]
        new_right = right if rcol_indexer is None else right.iloc[:, rcol_indexer]

        # GH#60498 For MultiIndex column alignment
        if isinstance(cols, MultiIndex):
            # When overwriting column names, make a shallow copy so as to not modify
            # the input DFs
            new_left = new_left.copy(deep=False)
            new_right = new_right.copy(deep=False)
            new_left.columns = cols
            new_right.columns = cols

        result = op(new_left, new_right)

        # Do the join on the columns instead of using left._align_for_op
        #  to avoid constructing two potentially large/sparse DataFrames
        join_columns = left.columns.join(right.columns, how="outer")

        if result.columns.has_duplicates:
            # Avoid reindexing with a duplicate axis.
            # https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/35194
            indexer, _ = result.columns.get_indexer_non_unique(join_columns)
            indexer = algorithms.unique1d(indexer)
            result = result._reindex_with_indexers(
                {1: [join_columns, indexer]}, allow_dups=True
            )
        elif (missing_cols := [c for c in join_columns if c not in result.columns]):
            # GH63288, Use pd.NA to fill missing values instead of np.nan
            # For columns that were not part of the inner operation result
            # (i.e. columns present in only one side), ensure we reintroduce
            # them with an appropriate nullable/pyarrow dtype rather than
            # allowing an upcast to numpy float with NaN. Build fill columns
            # using the original left/right dtypes as preference.
            # Create NA-filled columns using the original column dtype as
            # a preference: preserve extension dtypes (including
            # pyarrow-backed) and use float64 for plain numpy integer dtypes
            # so missing values are represented as ``NaN``.
            for col in missing_cols:
                src = left[col] if col in left.columns else right[col]

                if is_extension_array_dtype(src.dtype):
                    # Construct an empty Series with the same dtype and
                    # reindex it to produce a full-length NA Series that
                    # preserves the extension (including pyarrow) storage.
                    empty = src.iloc[:0]
                    fill = empty.reindex(result.index)
                else:
                    fill = left._constructor_sliced([np.nan] * len(result.index), index=result.index, dtype=np.float64)

                result[col] = fill

            result = result.reindex(join_columns, axis=1)

        return result


```

import pytest

def test_arith_preserve_pyarrow_int_missing_as_pdNA():
    """Regression test for GH#63288: arithmetic should preserve pyarrow-backed
    nullable integer dtypes and represent missing integer values as ``pd.NA``
    rather than numpy ``NaN`` when columns do not fully overlap.
    """
    import pandas as pd

    df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3], "b": [4, 5, 6], "c": [7, 8, 9]})
    df1 = df.iloc[:, :2].astype("Int64[pyarrow]")
    df2 = df.iloc[1:, 1:].astype("Int64[pyarrow]")

    res = df1 + df2

    # Expect the resulting integer columns to keep a pyarrow-backed integer dtype
    from pandas.api import types as ptypes

    assert getattr(res["a"].dtype, "storage", "") == "pyarrow"
    assert getattr(res["b"].dtype, "storage", "") == "pyarrow"
    assert ptypes.is_integer_dtype(res["a"].dtype)
    assert ptypes.is_integer_dtype(res["b"].dtype)

    # Missing positions should be represented by a pandas NA-like value
    # (we check for isna to allow extension array NA semantics)
    import pandas as _pd

    assert _pd.isna(res["a"].iat[0])
    assert _pd.isna(res["b"].iat[0])

This is intentional, because the new `str` dtype is a default dtype (and agnostic to it being backed by pyarrow, which is not required), while the `ArrowDtype` dtypes are opt-in dtypes. 

The reasoning is that when you use the default dtypes, standard operations should only result in other default dtypes, and you only get the optional (experimental) ArrowDtypes by an explicit action to get those (e.g. by reading with specifying dtype_backend keyword, or with `convert_dtypes()`).

If you want `<NA>` as the NA-sentinel, you can opt into the `string` dtype.

```python
t1 = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        'c0': ['aa'],
        'c1': ['bb']
    },
    dtype="string",
)
result = t1.assign(c0_t1=lambda df: df['c0'].where(t1['c0'].isin(['c1']), other=pd.NA))
print(result)
#    c0  c1 c0_t1
# 0  aa  bb  <NA>
```

You can recover 2.3.x behavior by setting `pd.set_option("future.infer_string", False)`, however this will eventually be going away.

> If converting pandas objects to pyarrow always create non-chunked arrow objects, then perhaps we should implement `__arrow_c_array__` instead?

For our numpy-based dtypes, this is indeed the case. But the problem is that for the pyarrow-based columns, we actually store chunked arrays. 

So when implementing one protocol, it should be `__arrow_c_stream__` I think. I am not entirely sure how helpful it would be to also implement `__arrow_c_array__` and let that either only work if there is only one chunk (and error otherwise) or let that concatenate implicitly when there are multiple chunks.

> So when implementing one protocol, it should be `__arrow_c_stream__` I think.

Yes that makes sense and I'd agree. I'd suggest always exporting a stream.

Why wouldn't we support both methods? The fact that pyarrow arrays use chunked storage behind the scenes is an implementation detail, but for everything else (and from a front-end perspective) array makes more sense than array_stream
N.B. I'm also not sure the decision that went into us using chunked array storage for pyarrow-backed types

I think the question is: what should data consumers be able to infer based on the presence of one or more of these methods. See https://github.com/apache/arrow/issues/40648

- If an object implements `__arrow_c_array__`, then the object's internal storage should already be contiguous. You shouldn't implement `__arrow_c_array__` if calling that would (even sometimes) require a concatenation to happen. 
- If an object's internal storage may be one or more arrays, then it should implement `__arrow_c_stream__`, where the stream will sometimes include only a single array, but where it can be zero-copy as much as possible (in the pandas case: always except from non-arrow storage)

There is still some discussion about using array vs stream interface, so reopening this issue.

@WillAyd 's comment from https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/59587#issuecomment-2311278954:

> To talk more practically, I am wondering about a scenario where we have a series that holds a chunked array. In this PR, we convert that to a singular array before then exposing it back as a stream, but the other point of view is that we could allow the stream to iterate over each chunk.
> 
> But then the question becomes what happens when that same Series gets used in a Dataframe? Does the dataframe iterate its chunks? In most cases, it seems highly unlikely that this is possible (unless all other Series of the Dataframe share the same chunked array size), so you get a rather interesting scenario where iterating by dataframe could be potentially far more expensive than the Series iteration.

For the specific example of a Series with multiple chunks, and then put in a DataFrame: if you access that through the DataFrame's stream interface, you will also get multiple chunks.

In pyarrow, a Table is also not required to have equally chunked columns, but when converting to a stream of batches, it will kind of merge the chunking of the different columns (I think by default in such a way that everything can be zero-copy slices from the original data, i.e. so the smallest batches needed to do that for all columns).

Another consideration point is how we want to act as consumers of Arrow data, not just as a producer. If we push developers towards preferring stream data in this interface, the implication is that as a consumer we would need to prefer Arrow chunked array storage for our arrays.

My general position is that PyCapsule Interface producers should not make it unintentionally easy to force memory copies. So if a pandas series could be either chunked or non-chunked, then only the C Stream interface should be implemented. Otherwise, implementing the C Array interface as well could allow consumers to unknowingly cause pandas to concatenate a series into an array.

IMO, the C Array interface should only be implemented if a pandas Series _always_ stores a contiguous array under the hood. It's easy for consumers of a C stream to see if the stream only holds a single array (assuming the consumer materializes the full stream)

Just an update, it seems like the current implementation is running into difficulty due to the value contrast between numbers being too large. There is a compensation number which works as a fallback to catch the changes in the small numbers, but because the data set here includes two equally large magnitudes (1e6, -1e6), the algorithm overwrites the compensation number which is what causes  a knock-on effect for the running summation of x^4.

```

`======================================================== short test summary info =========================================================
FAILED pandas/tests/arrays/sparse/test_array.py::TestSparseArrayAnalytics::test_cumsum[True-data1-expected1] - AssertionError: numpy array are different
FAILED pandas/tests/arrays/sparse/test_array.py::TestSparseArrayAnalytics::test_cumsum[False-data1-expected1] - AssertionError: numpy array are different`

After looking into this, two observations:

_Why didn't the tests fail bc of infinite recursion before?_ 
Both test cases use float dtype, which makes the fill value nan, so the code does not go to the recursive branch.

_Why do the tests fail after the above patch is applied?_ 
The cumsum output is different for numpy and SparseArray, when dealing with nan (note that the tests only fail for data1 and expected1, which has nan). Namely, SparseArray cumsum should "ignore" the nan, according to its docstring, while numpy propagates it to the remaining indices. 
```
>>> np.array([1,np.nan,3], dtype=float).cumsum()
array([ 1., nan, nan])
>>> SparseArray([1,np.nan,3], dtype=float).cumsum()
[1.0, nan, 4.0]
```

So, when you apply the above patch, `self.to_dense()` first converts the SparseArray into a numpy array. Then, calling `.cumsum()` does it like numpy does, i.e., propagates the nan to the rest of the indices, and so the result does not match the expected one. A fix would have to maintain this skip-nan property, which I am not sure how to yet.

```python
from typing import reveal_type
import pandas as pd
from datetime import timedelta

# Base numeric index
idx = pd.Index([1, 2, 3])

# Works correctly because pandas can broadcast a single timedelta value.

# Useful if you want to preserve the index type for downstream operations.
r4 = pd.to_timedelta(idx.to_series() * pd.to_timedelta(timedeltas))
reveal_type(r4)  # TimedeltaIndex

To illustrate the issue with a small pure python example (what I originally used to explore the implementation), consider the following class that wraps some underlying data and allows to get/set data:

```python
import sys

class Object:
    """Small class that wraps some data, and can get/set this data"""
    
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data = data
    
    def __getitem__(self, key):
        return Object(self.data[key])
    
    def __setitem__(self, key, value):
        print("Refcount self: ", sys.getrefcount(self))
        self.data[key] = value
    
    def __repr__(self):
        return f"<Object {self.data}>"
    
    def copy(self):
        return Object(self.data.copy())
```

and then setting some data with Python 3.13:

```python
>>> obj = Object(list(range(10)))
# direct setitem -> this modifies the underlying data
>>> obj[5] = 100
Refcount self:  4
>>> obj
<Object [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 100, 6, 7, 8, 9]>

# chained setitem -> this does NOT modify the underlying data
# (in this toy example because the slice of a list gives a new list, not a view)
>>> obj[1:4][1] = 1000
Refcount self:  3
>>> obj
<Object [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 100, 6, 7, 8, 9]>
```

Running that with Python 3.14:

```python
>>> obj = Object(list(range(10)))
>>> obj[5] = 100
Refcount self:  4
>>> obj[1:4][1] = 1000
Refcount self:  2
```

So that already illustrates that there is a difference in this basic example. 
Although the fact that it is _lower_ in the case of chained assignment, that is not really a problem given we test for `<=3`, but the problem I suppose is that there are also other cases where the refcount becomes lower, giving false positive warnings.

Testing that with code that is not run top-level in the interactive interpreter, but is code in a function that is called, we can already see this. When running the below example with a non-chained assignment in a test with Python 3.13, that gives a refcount of 4 as well, i.e. the same regardless of whether it is in a function or not. But with Python 3.14, the below code no longer gives a refcount of 4, but only of 2:

```python
>>> def test():
...     obj = Object(list(range(10)))
...     obj[5] = 100
... 
>>> test()
Refcount self:  2
```

And so if the above `obj` would be a pandas DataFrame, and we are doing a plain setitem operation in the function, that currently triggers a false positive warning, unfortunately.

Based on the above, I assume the simple conclusion is that the current implementation for the warning check using `sys.getrefcount(self)` will no longer work, and there is not really any other alternative than to disable the warning for Python 3.14+ ..

I am of the opinion that indexing with a label list should not behave any differently than indexing with an equivalent boolean array (when an equivalent boolean array exists), and this is currently not the case with `unsorted_s.loc[:, sorted_labels]`. Perhaps I am alone here, but I most often use

* `unsorted_s.loc[:, sorted_labels]` as a shorthand for `unsorted_s.loc[unsorted_s.index.get_level_values(0), sorted_labels]`
* `unsorted_s.loc[:, labels1, labels2]` as a shorthand for `unsorted_s.loc[unsorted_s.index.isin(labels1, 1) & unsorted_s.index.isin(labels2, 2)]` or `unsorted_s.loc[unsorted_s.index.droplevel().isin(pd.MultiIndex.from_product([labels1, labels2]))]`
* *etc.*

(As an aside, it seems rather odd to me that `MultiIndex.isin` cannot operate on a selection of levels.)

and I would expect a lot of people who also work with a lot of raw NumPy arrays would expect it to function as such. But besides that, the real pain point for me is that it does so *inconsistently* depending on invisible factors like which function mapped the labels to codes. If you don't want to rely on private members like `_lexsort_depth`, you have to jump through a lot of hoops to programmatically determine how the result will be ordered. The `error` is caused by the slice and it actually is not an error.  When you use slicing operations like `[::-1]` in pandas/NumPy, it creates a view of the original data rather than a new array. This view has the following characteristics:

- It references the same memory as the original array
- It uses a negative stride to traverse the elements in reverse order
- It becomes non-contiguous in memory

1. C-contiguous: Data elements are stored sequentially in memory (row by row)
2. Non-contiguous: Data elements are not stored sequentially, requiring jumps in memory when accessing them in order

To solve it, just call `.copy()` on the dataframe. 
It will allocates new memory and creates a fresh array with the data arranged in proper C-contiguous order

PS: 
- PyArrow-backed arrays typically materialize a new copy when slicing operations occur
- This happens automatically behind the scenes, creating a properly formatted array

The issue is from two optimizations pandas is using, one in apply_frame_axis0 and one in copy. apply_frame_axis0 is essentially reusing an index object to avoid having to recreate for each group. Care is taken if a user is detected modifying the index, but not if a user stores the index (in this case, inside of a DataFrame).

Axes should be widely thought as immutable (even if the pandas internals don't), as so within DataFrame.copy we have:

https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/7d2f5ce59551a52643318f3e4e9cd1b8058a6e44/pandas/core/internals/managers.py#L816-L822

Running the code with `.copy(deep="all")` resolves the issue, but I believe this is not documented and should be considered internal; users shouldn't rely on it.

As for how to resolve the issue, it's a bit unclear to me. I wonder if it would be palatable to have an internal flag on an Index object like `_recycled` that could be detected in copy (and elsewhere?) that would inform copy to copy the axis.

Hi @Dvdandrades, thanks for the clarification and for referencing #63138.

I think there is an important distinction in how TOON formats **object** vs **tabular** structures. Based on the official TOON spec, the correct outputs should be:

---

### **1. Object Type**

**Input:**

```
{
  "name": ["Ali", "Sara"],
  "age": [23, 21]
}
```

**Correct TOON Output:**

```
name[2]: Ali,Sara
age[2]: 23,21
```

This is the expected behavior because TOON treats this as a **flat object with array fields**, not a row-major table.

---

### **2. Tabular Type**

**Input:**

```
[
  {
    "name": ["Ali", "Sara"],
    "age": [23, 21]
  }
]
```

**Correct TOON Output:**

```
[1]:
  - name[2]: Ali,Sara
    age[2]: 23,21
```

Here TOON interprets the outer list as a **tabular array**, so the structure is wrapped with `[1]:`.

---

**For More Examples:**
File: `data.toon`
```
[2]:
  - id: 1
    name: Alice
    scores[3]: 85,90,95
    details:
      age: 20
      city: New York
  - id: 2
    name: Bob
    scores[3]: 78,82,88
    details:
      age: 22
      city: Los Angeles
```
**My achievement output:**

```
========== data.toon to DataFrame( to_read) ==========


   id   name    scores  details.age details.city
0   1  Alice  85,90,95           20     New York
1   2    Bob  78,82,88           22  Los Angeles

[2 rows x 5 columns]

========== DataFrame Info ==========

{'table_name': None, 'lengthMarker': None, 'N': 2, 'delimiter': ',', 'format_type': 'tabular_array', 'flatten_nested': True, 'nested_depth': 0}

========== Columns ==========

Index(['id', 'name', 'scores', 'details.age', 'details.city'], dtype='str')

========== Data Types ==========

id              int64
name              str
scores            str
details.age     int64
details.city      str
Length: 5, dtype: object

 ======= pandas.DataFrame to_toon output ==========


[2]:
  - id: 1
    name: Alice
    scores[3]: 85,90,95
    details:
      age: 20
      city: New York
  - id: 2
    name: Bob
    scores[3]: 78,82,88
    details:
      age: 22
      city: Los Angeles
```
### Why this distinction matters

TOON can be **unstructured**, which is why the spec includes multiple encoding types:

* primitive
* object
* tabular-array
* mixed

For this reason, DataFrame ↔︎ TOON conversion must correctly detect and preserve TOON structure instead of forcing a row-major format.

I’ve already implemented full support for both **tabular TOON → DataFrame** and **DataFrame → TOON** (including mixed nested cases). Please refer to my issue  [#63153](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/63153) for details — happy to contribute this as a PR if maintainers think it aligns with pandas I/O patterns.

Hi @MuhammadUsman-Khan , thanks for creating this issue — I want to clarify an important point regarding the expected TOON format shown here.

The TOON output in your example is **not aligned with the actual TOON specification**. TOON treats *object*, *tabular*, and *mixed* structures differently, so the formatting changes depending on the JSON structure.

For example, for input like:

```
{
  "name": ["Ali", "Sara"],
  "age": [23, 21]
}
```

the correct TOON format is:

```
name[2]: Ali,Sara
age[2]: 23,21
```

But if the input is a tabular array:

```
[
  {
    "name": ["Ali", "Sara"],
    "age": [23, 21]
  }
]
```

the correct TOON format becomes:

```
[1]:
  - name[2]: Ali,Sara
    age[2]: 23,21
```

So the “expected output” you mentioned doesn’t match the official TOON encoding rules.

I’ve already implemented a fully working TOON reader/writer for tabular format and the rest of all types (like object) on running and shared it in my issue here:
**👉  #63153 
This version correctly handles any kind of TOON structure and converts it to/from pandas DataFrames.

Feel free to check it out—happy to collaborate or refine the behavior if needed.

For rationale, pasting Tom's comment from the PR here:

> > General question - is this behavior defined or standardized somewhere?
> 
> It's part of some IEEE spec, but I haven't tracked down the source. Both Python and NumPy use this behavior for NaN.
> 
> For NA, I think it aligns with the principles behind Kleene logic. `True | NA` is True, since `True | anything` is True. Similarly, `NA ** 0` is 1, since `anything ** 0` is 1.

And from the issue:

> I think our invariant is that NA represents unknown. So if you have an operation that is know with only one operand, like “True | NA”, then the output should be known and not NA.

---

Personally, I think this is a case where there are valid arguments both ways, and choosing one will always make some people unhappy (a bit like the sum of empty being 0 vs NA case, but then on a smaller scale ;)). 
Always propagating nulls in arithmetic operations gives a simpler behaviour (and implementation), while returning a non-NA value if the result can be known is more in line with the boolean operators (Kleene logic).

But given that most of the comparable tools nowadays follow the "always propagate" case for arithmetic, that feels like a good reason to go for that as well (if there are no strong reasons otherwise to pick the other behaviour).

I'm +1 for this change to align with the broader ecosystem of tools.

Since NA is a mask over valued data that indicates missingness, I do not think it should be held to the rules of an algebraic system. The concept of missingness is agnostic to the underlying data type, and there is ambiguity as to what the intuitive result should be. For example, there is no strong formal argument for whether `NA ** 0` should evaluate to `1` or `NA` which can be seen as a trade-off between convenience and formalism.

This raises the counter-argument of why boolean comparisons involving `Null` are treated differently. As we could use either Kleene logic or "Always return Null" logic. Historically Kleene logic has been used because it preserves logical identities while also producing more intuitive query results.

```python
import duckdb

res = duckdb.sql('''
    with employees as (
        SELECT *
        FROM (
            VALUES
                ('Alice', 5),
                ('Bob', NULL),
                ('Carol', 7)
        ) AS t(employee, manager_id)
    )

    select * from employees
    where (manager_id = 5) or (manager_id is NULL);
''')

# Kleene logic returns rows for Alice and Bob
print(res)
# ┌──────────┬────────────┐
# │ employee │ manager_id │
# │ varchar  │   int32    │
# ├──────────┼────────────┤
# │ Bob      │       NULL │
# │ Alice    │          5 │
# └──────────┴────────────┘

# Always Null logic would (surprisingly?) only return Alice
# without Kleene logic, Null or True returns Null which is filtered out.
# ┌──────────┬────────────┐
# │ employee │ manager_id │
# │ varchar  │   int32    │
# ├──────────┼────────────┤
# │ Alice    │          5 │
# └──────────┴────────────┘
```

### Findings:

There are actually *two* things going on:

1. The mapping behavior with `defaultdict` / `na_action`
2. The fact that converting to `category` changes the *scalar* representation of missing values from `<NA>` to `NaN`

The second part is independent of the `na_val = ...` logic in `Categorical.map`.

So for row 2:

* `c[2]` is `<NA>` with type `pandas._libs.missing.NAType`
* `d[2]` is `NaN` with type `float`

This happens even if the mapping itself handles NA “correctly” in terms of `isna()` – the moment the column is `dtype="category"`, the scalar missing becomes `np.nan` instead of `pd.NA`.

As far as I can tell:

* This is **by design** for `Categorical`: internally, missing is stored as code `-1`, and when we pull a scalar from a categorical with a missing entry, pandas returns `np.nan`.
* For object / nullable dtypes, the scalar missing is `pd.NA`.

So the NA → NaN change I’m seeing after `astype("category")` is not caused by:

```
na_val = mapper(np.nan) if callable(mapper) else mapper.get(np.nan, np.nan)
```

It’s categorical’s scalar representation of missing values.

If we want ```df["d"] = df["d"].map(defaultdict(lambda: True), na_action="ignore")``` to return `pd.NA` instead of `np.nan`, that would mean changing categorical’s public scalar API to use `pd.NA` as the missing sentinel. That’s a bigger design change with potential compatibility impact, since a lot of existing code currently expects `np.nan` when accessing missing values from categoricals.

So my understanding is:

* For this specific issue, the main bug is the **mapping behavior** (dict-like mappers, `na_action`, etc.).
* The NA → NaN change after `astype("category")` is part of the existing categorical design: missing scalars from categoricals are `np.nan`, not `pd.NA`.

### Possible change

One way to make the dict-like path behave more like the callable path (and respect defaultdict / __missing__) would be to use __getitem__ instead of .get for Mapping objects, falling back to np.nan on KeyError:

```
if na_action is None and has_nans:
      if na_action is None and has_nans:
          if callable(mapper):
              na_val = mapper(np.nan)
          elif isinstance(mapper, Mapping):
              try:
                  # Use __getitem__ so defaultdict.__missing__ is honored
                  na_val = mapper[np.nan]
              except KeyError:
                  na_val = np.nan
          else:
              na_val = np.nan
```


This would:

- keep callable behavior exactly the same
- keep plain dict behavior the same, unless there is an explicit np.nan key
- fix the defaultdict case so that np.nan actually maps via the default factory (e.g. to True in the example above) instead of silently turning into None → NaN.


```python
import pandas as pd
from collections import defaultdict
import numpy as np

df = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "a": ["one", "two", pd.NA],
        "b": ["one", "two", pd.NA],
        "c": ["one", "two", pd.NA],
        "d": ["one", "two", pd.NA],
    }
)

# Make b and d categorical up front
df["b"] = df["b"].astype("category")
df["d"] = df["d"].astype("category")

mapper = defaultdict(lambda: True)

df["a"] = df["a"].map(mapper, na_action=None)
df["b"] = df["b"].map(mapper, na_action=None)
df["c"] = df["c"].map(mapper, na_action="ignore")
df["d"] = df["d"].map(mapper, na_action="ignore")

print(df)
print(df.applymap(type))

assert not df["a"].isna().any()
assert not df["b"].isna().any()

```

1  True  True  True  True
2  True  True  <NA>   NaN
<sys>:0: FutureWarning: DataFrame.applymap has been deprecated. Use DataFrame.map instead.
                a               b                                      c                d
0  <class 'bool'>  <class 'bool'>                         <class 'bool'>   <class 'bool'>
1  <class 'bool'>  <class 'bool'>                         <class 'bool'>   <class 'bool'>
2  <class 'bool'>  <class 'bool'>  <class 'pandas._libs.missing.NAType'>  <class 'float'>

In 
```
na_val = mapper(np.nan) if callable(mapper) else mapper.get(np.nan, np.nan)
```
When pandas builds the result Series for b:

- non-NA rows ("one", "two") get mapped via mapper[...] → True
- NA row uses na_val → None

So we end up with something like:

[True, True, None]

When pandas wraps that into a Series, it has to pick a dtype:

True + None → cannot be pure bool, so it promotes to an object/float combo. None is represented as NaN for that dtype

In the new code

When pandas builds the result:

- non-NA rows: "one", "two" → True
- NA row: use na_val → True

So the mapped values for b are:

[True, True, True]

There is no None anymore, so nothing gets turned into NaN.

**Questions / Next Steps**

I have two questions about how to proceed with a fix:

### **1. Is it appropriate to open a PR with the updated `na_val` logic?**

The current behavior comes from:

```python
na_val = mapper(np.nan) if callable(mapper) else mapper.get(np.nan, np.nan)
```

For dict-like mappers (especially `defaultdict`), using `.get()` bypasses the default factory, so:

```python
defaultdict(lambda: True).get(np.nan)   # -> None
```

This results in the NA position becoming `None` → `NaN` when constructing the categorical output.

With the patched version:

```python
if callable(mapper):
    na_val = mapper(np.nan)
elif isinstance(mapper, Mapping):
    try:
        na_val = mapper[np.nan]   # honors defaultdict.__missing__
    except KeyError:
        na_val = np.nan
else:
    na_val = np.nan
```

the NA position now correctly maps to the mapper’s default value (`True` in this example), which aligns categorical behavior with `Series.map` on non-categorical dtypes.

### **2. Should `astype("category")` be changed to preserve `pd.NA` instead of converting it to `np.nan`?**

* For object/nullable → `pd.NA`
* For categorical → `np.nan` (float scalar)

This behavior is independent of the `map` logic—it comes from how categorical handles missing codes internally.

By constructing the DataFrame with lists containing a `None`, `DataFrame.__init__` will eventually lead down [this code path](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/a609b57b580b823890e272fdae666b8dc796a057/pandas/_libs/lib.pyx#L2864-L2872) when inferring types for the columns. The local variable `ints` would contain the expected result, but because `convert_to_nullable_dtype` defaults to False, it will fall back to the `float64` array. Then, calling `df.convert_dtypes` will call [`np.ndarray.astype(int)`](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.ndarray.astype.html) on the `float64` array, which raises the warning.

The proposed `(s[0] == s).all()` is error-prone in edge cases (What if s[0] is NaN? What if s is empty?), and actually slower for small Series. Going this route, one should do a `.dropna()` and `.values`/`.array` first.

I posted my finding here: https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/issues/11910. However, this solution is still O(N) and not short-circuiting. For large Series that are non-constant with high likelihood, naive python code can be orders of magnitude faster. 

```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

def is_constant(array):
    if len(array) <= 1:
        return True
    first = array[0]
    return all(item == first for item in array)

const = pd.Series(np.ones(1_000_000)).values
irreg = pd.Series(np.random.randn(1_000_000)).values

%timeit is_constant(const)         # 72.7 ms ± 1.66 ms 
%timeit (const[0] == const).all()  # 144 µs ± 2.3 µs
%timeit is_constant(irreg)         # 968 ns ± 6.7 ns
%timeit (irreg[0] == irreg).all()  # 129 µs ± 132 ns
```

With numba-jit we can further drastically improve the performance

```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import numba

@numba.njit
def is_constant(array):
    if len(array) <= 1:
        return True
    first = array[0]
    for item in array:
        if item != first:
            return False
    return True

const = pd.Series(np.ones(1_000_000)).values
irreg = pd.Series(np.random.randn(1_000_000)).values

%timeit is_constant(const)         # 457 µs ± 5.42 µs  (instead of 72 ms)
%timeit (const[0] == const).all()  # 136 µs ± 311 ns
%timeit is_constant(irreg)         # 242 ns ± 1.52 ns  (instead of 968 ns)
%timeit (irreg[0] == irreg).all()  # 128 µs ± 2.15 µs
```

> I recognize I'm late to this, but out of curiosity, why use pyarrow string arrays instead of using numpy structured types for unicode strings (e.g., `dtype='<U12'` or whatever length)?

NumPy only supports rectangular arrays of strings.  So '<U12" requires 12*4 bytes  (used UTF-32 encoding) for every entry irrespective of size or the characters used.  More efficient storage methods use ragged arrays where usually 2 things are stores in the array, a memory address of the actual UTF8 string and the length of the string.  Consider the sime example

```
a
abcdefghijkl
```

In NumPy this array requires 96 buytes for storage (+ overheads).  In an efficient encoding this requires something on the order of 1 (a) + 8 (memory address) + 8 (length, assuming int64) + 12 (other string) + 8 + 8 = 45, which is about 50%.  If an array is very sparse (say has one very long string, and the rest short, then the ratio os space required can get really bad).

NumPy is working on 1st party support for ragged UTF strings in NumPy 2.0(ish) which requires a new way to define dtypes..

### Integrate with GCP bucket
- Pandas accept URLs with the prefix "gcs://", and will use gcsfs to complete the IO operation.

**Write DataFrame to Google Cloud Storage**

df.to_pickle('gs://bucket-name/path/file-name.pkl', <other parameters>,  storage_options={"token": "credentials.json"})

**Read DataFrame from Google Cloud Storage**
```
df.read_pickle('gs://bucket-name/path/file-name.pkl', <other parameters>,  storage_options={"token": "credentials.json"})

This might be due to now passing an object dtype array to numpy (related to my comment at https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/62040#issuecomment-3378169117, second-to-last bullet point at the bottom of that comment). So either we should change that back to float with NaNs, or explicitly choose the float with NaN conversion under the hood in `__array_ufunc__`. 
(I think generally almost none of the builtin numpy ufuncs will be able to work on object dtype array)

> I'd have expected `[True, False, NA]`

That's reasonable, but my intuition would be `[True, False, False]`, and specifically return an ndarray[bool].  Anyone else have strong opinions here, cc @jorisvandenbossche ?

FWIW: In Kleene logic, NOT NULL -> NULL (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three-valued_logic#Kleene_and_Priest_logics), so I think the expectation of keeping NA for isnan would make sense.

Basically, we're asking "is this unknown value NaN?" and the answer is "I don't know. it could be. it could not be. the value is unknown".

I think the general rule is that NA values always propagate in element-wise functions (certainly for a generic ufunc where we might not know what it is doing exactly, for the reason @twast outlined), except for a function that specifically checks for NA (isna/notna).

> specifically return an ndarray[bool]

That might be a bigger question for our ufunc support, but by implementing `__array_ufunc__` we ensure to wrap the result again in a pandas object. Starting to return an ndarray seems like a big deviation from that (and is something we should consider in general, not for a single ufunc).

TL;DR There turns out to be a missing `break` statement inside `lib.maybe_convert_objects`.  Posting the rest of the tracking-this-down process for pedagogical purposes:

Drilling down on where the time is spent (`%prun` isn't giving very useful info for me, i suspect bc most of the time is spent in cython)

```
n = 10**6
arr1 = np.repeat(pd.Timestamp('2019-01-01 00:00:00', tz=None), n)
arr2 = np.repeat(pd.Timestamp('2019-01-01 00:00:00', tz='UTC'), n)

In [75]: %timeit a = pd.Series(arr1)
359 ms ± 1.47 ms per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 1 loop each)

In [76]: %timeit b = pd.Series(arr2)
198 ms ± 2.26 ms per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 1 loop each)
```

So its only 1.8x for me, which is a lot better than 6x.  Drilling down further:

```
In [77]: %timeit a = pd.core.construction.sanitize_array(arr1, None)
367 ms ± 17.4 ms per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 1 loop each)

In [78]: %timeit b = pd.core.construction.sanitize_array(arr2, None)
196 ms ± 1.62 ms per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 1 loop each)
```

Which confirms that effectively all the time is spent inside sanitize_array.  More:

```
In [80]: %timeit a = pd._libs.lib.maybe_convert_objects(arr1, convert_non_numeric=True)
356 ms ± 6.03 ms per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 1 loop each)

In [81]: %timeit b = pd._libs.lib.maybe_convert_objects(arr2, convert_non_numeric=True)
198 ms ± 797 μs per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 1 loop each)
```

Again effectively all the time.  Next, inside maybe_convert_objects these go down different paths, paraphrasing:

```
    if seen.datetimetz_:  # <- tzaware case
        if is_datetime_with_singletz_array(objects):  
    elif seen.datetime_:  # <- tznaive case
        if is_datetime_or_datetime64_array(objects):
```

So we guess that either the DatetimeIndex call is the difference, or the is_datetime_yadda_yadda.  To check this we need to change the `cdef is_datetime_or_datetime64_array` to cpdef, then:

```
In [6]: %timeit pd._libs.lib.is_datetime_with_singletz_array(arr2)
94.4 ms ± 1.53 ms per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 10 loops each)

%timeit pd._libs.lib.is_datetime_or_datetime64_array(arr1)
93.4 ms ± 839 μs per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 10 loops each)
```

Then the DatetimeIndex constructor:

```
In [82]: %timeit a = pd.DatetimeIndex(arr1)
52.7 ms ± 1.16 ms per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 10 loops each)

In [83]: %timeit b = pd.DatetimeIndex(arr2)
106 ms ± 453 μs per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 10 loops each)
```

OK, we're on to something!  the is_datetime_foo calls were the same speed and the DatetimeIndex calls were actually _faster_ for the tznaive case.  So something must be amiss inside lib.maybe_convert_objects _before_ we get to the is_datetime_foo calls.  Looking up at the code that sets `seen.datetimetz` and `seen.datetime_`:

```
        elif PyDateTime_Check(val) or cnp.is_datetime64_object(val):

            # if we have a tz's attached then return the objects
            if convert_non_numeric:
                if getattr(val, "tzinfo", None) is not None:
                    seen.datetimetz_ = True
                    break
                else:
                    seen.datetime_ = True
                    try:
                        convert_to_tsobject(val, None, None, 0, 0)
                    except OutOfBoundsDatetime:
                        # e.g. test_out_of_s_bounds_datetime64
                        seen.object_ = True
                        break
```

The alert reader will note a missing `break` in the tznaive not-of-bounds case.  Adding that `break`:

```
In [4]: %timeit a = pd.Series(arr1)
152 ms ± 2.12 ms per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 10 loops each)

In [5]: %timeit b = pd.Series(arr2)
211 ms ± 9.89 ms per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 1 loop each)
```

Ta-da!

This current momentum rolling method is not able to get high precision when data ranges abnormally. The same to #47461.

maybe an ad hoc for `rolling().std()` when data ranges abnormally is  `rolling.agg(lambda x: np.std(x, ddof=1))`:
```
df.rolling(6).agg(lambda x: np.std(x, ddof=1))[-1:]

15  1.643168
```

The reason why the `rolling().std()` and `tail().std() `methods in pandas are returning different results because they are using different window sizes to calculate the standard deviation.

In the case of `df.data.rolling(6).std()[-1:]`, a rolling window of size 6 is used to calculate the standard deviation, which includes the outlier value of 10 billion. This causes the standard deviation to be much larger than when the outlier is excluded.

On the other hand, `df.data.tail(6).std()` only considers the last 6 values in the DataFrame, excluding the outlier value. This results in a smaller standard deviation compared to when the outlier is included.

To ensure that the results are equal, you can use the same window size for both methods by using `df.data.tail(6).rolling(6).std()[-1:]`. This will calculate the standard deviation for the last 6 values of the data frame using a rolling window of size 6, which includes the outlier value.

Alternatively, you can remove the outlier value from the DataFrame before calculating the standard deviation using the drop method, like so:

```
df_without_outlier = df.drop(df.loc[df['data'] == 10000000000].index)
df_without_outlier.rolling(6).std()[-1:]
```
This will remove the outlier value from the DataFrame and then calculate the standard deviation using a rolling window of size 6, resulting in a smaller standard deviation value that is more in line with the `tail().std()` method.

What about the following set of arguments to both `to_sql` and `get_schema` (or whatever that method is eventually called):
- `frame` - DataFrame
- `name` - table name
- `con` - connection object
- `schema` - database schema (yes, definitely confusing viz-a-viz `get_schema` --- let's rename for sure)
- `if_exists` - Not sure if this should be a parameter to `get_schema` also, or if that should just always return the creation code (even if table exists)
- `index` - Whether to add index as a column or not. Default True
- `primary_keys` - Which column(s) to make the primary key. Can be a single string or a list of strings. Defaults to no primary keys.
- `sql_indexes` - Which columns to index. Can be a single string (e.g. `'name'` -> `name` column is indexed), a list of strings (e.g. `['name','title']` -> `name` column is indexed, `title` column is indexed) or a list of lists of strings (e.g. `[ ['name','title'], ]` -> `(name, title)` are indexed jointly).  If `index=True`, defaults to making the DataFrame index column.  If DataFrame has multi-index, all multi-index series are indexed jointly (_notice_ that this is different from current behavior: IIRC, currently the columns of a multi-index would be indexed separately)
- `unique_sql_indexes` - Same as `sql_indexes` but for creating indexes w/ UNIQUE constraint. Defaults to no unique indexes.
- `foreign_keys` - Dict of form `{'column': ('OtherTable','id'), 'column2':('OtherTable2','id'), ...}`
- `dtype` - Dictionary of column to dtype mappings.

I tried to reproduce this error.  In concat's _make_concat_multiindex (when all input indexes are the same and the inner index is not a MultiIndex), we build the result with:
- levels = [new_index.unique()] and
- codes = new_index.unique().get_indexer(new_index)

This assigns a non-negative code to <NA> and includes <NA> in levels. MultiIndex invariants expect "missing-at-row" to
be encoded as -1 in codes (and not as a category in levels), which is what get_loc/engines rely on for NA lookup. The
mismatch leads to the KeyError on ('a', pd.NA).

I think the minimal fix would be to use factorize_from_iterable(new_index) in that branch so NA is encoded as -1 and excluded from levels, matching our invariant and the "not-all-indexes-same" branch.

Related but separate edge case: NA in keys (outermost level) when levels=None and keys is 1-D, also keeps NA as a category today. If desired, we can mirror the same approach for keys (either factorize keys or remap NA key codes to -1) in a follow-up.

With `.loc` indexing in place replacement still depends on the uniqueness of the column names:

``` python
df = pd.DataFrame.from_items([(0, [0]), (0, [0]), ('foo', ['replace_me'])])
df.loc[:,'foo'].replace({'replace_me': 0}, inplace=True)
print(df)
```

```
    0  0         foo
0  0  0  replace_me
```

`df['foo']` returns a Series which _may_ have its data as a view. Modifying it in place doesn't ALWAYS propogate it back to the parent object. That's why this warning is there (or raise if you set the option). You should never do this, nor is their ever a reason to do so.

Simply assign the column as you would normally. If you really want to reset a non-unique column you can use `.iloc`.

You don't really want to work with non-unique columns if you can help. Its not very efficient and prob some lurking bugs. Use a multi-index if you really have non-unique data that is uniquely represented in mulit-levels.

```
